Do you have the direction how to analyze and select and how to write the reason for new task?

Yes. Here's the process I'll follow for each new task. It's built from prompt.md, Feedback.md and what the earlier review folders showed.

**1. Analyze**
- **Set up:** read the "User request" in the task HTML. Map the tabs to the files: the first iframe is Website A (saved_resource.html) and the second is Website B (saved_resource(1).html).
- **Full-size pass (1440px):** take full-page screenshots and note console errors. Go through the request point by point and check whether each one is actually there. For example: 5-year range, hover price, event bubbles, brand logo, single page.
- **Review-frame pass (sandboxed iframe, 1000×800, real mouse only):** this is how reviewers see the sites.
  - Click every button, tab, filter, toggle, card and tile, and record what each one does. Note anything that does nothing.
  - Hover every tooltip or bubble and check that the card appears and fits inside the frame.
  - Note any download that's blocked. Chrome blocks them all in the frame, even when the site says "downloaded".
- **Close-up pass:** screenshot each item in any gallery or collection. Look for overlapping text, clipped labels, wrong axis labels and low-contrast text.
- **Keep only flaws that show at every width.** Drop anything that only appears at one size or on a phone.

**2. Select**
- **Aesthetics:** visual quality only, meaning layout, typography, color, polish and visible defects like overlaps or broken labels.
- **Functionality:** behavior plus how well the site follows the request. That covers working versus dead controls, missing requested features, and extra views the request said not to add. A site that fails to load or freezes counts as a functionality failure.
- **Overall:** weigh both. It can differ from either of the other picks.
- **Ties:** use "Both are good" or "Both are bad" only for a real tie. A download blocked on both sites is a wash, not a reason to pick one.

**3. Write each reason**
- **Opening:** state the verdict with the site named in full, such as "Website A is better because…", "…is preferred…", "…is stronger…" or "…is the best option…".
- **Voice:** third person only, with no "I", "me" or "for me". Name both Website A and Website B in full.
- **Functionality evidence:** name each control and its result ("the Earnings chip shows 10 bubbles"). Count options and name dead controls; never write "fewer" or "more limited".
- **Aesthetics evidence:** specific details, such as which element, which color, and where it overlaps.
- **Overall comes last.** Weigh one visual point against one behavior point, and don't repeat the Functionality reason.
- **Claims:** only what holds in the review frame. No download claims unless one was confirmed there, and no phone claims. Say "the requested design" rather than "prompt" or "user request".
- **Style:** everyday spoken English with no em dashes. Use different openings from the previous task.
- **Length:** 60 words each, counted before handing over. prompt.md says 40–50, but you asked for 60 on the star task. Tell me if you want 40–50 instead.
- **Format:** one code block per reason, laid out as in prompt.md.

**4. Final check:** verdict first, both sites named, third person, word count, no download or phone claims, Overall weighs visual against behavior, every claim seen in the frame.

User request
Create a clean low-poly 3D model of a large format banner printing machine.
The machine should look like a professional vinyl / flex banner printer used in digital printing shops.
Design style:
minimal, modern, clean, low-poly 3D model suitable for website hero section.
Machine details:
• wide format industrial printer
• long horizontal printer body
• large vinyl banner roll coming out from the front
• visible rollers and print head area
• side control panel with small screen and buttons
• metal frame stand with wheels
• support rods holding the banner roll
Banner details:
• flexible vinyl banner sheet coming out of the printer
• slightly curved / flowing banner sheet
• colorful gradient printed design on the banner
• banner hanging naturally
Color theme:
• printer body: white and light grey
• accents: red or blue
• banner print: colorful gradient (pink, yellow, cyan)
Lighting:
soft studio lighting
subtle shadows
clean background
Rendering style:
isometric 3D
website UI friendly
product showcase style
Animation readiness:
object centered
balanced proportions
optimized for slow rotation animation
Technical requirements:
• low polygon count
• lightweight model
• optimized for WebGL / Three.js
• suitable for interactive website
Output:
single 3D object
transparent or neutral background
clean geometry

content.text:
The decision is clear, with one correction to my earlier notes. Website A's accent is #ee613b and Website B's coral is #e95743, which are nearly the same red-orange. So I won't count the accent color against Website A. The difference is that Website B also offers a cobalt blue option.

Website B wins all three for 6241898. Website A is "Forma 1600" (saved_resource.html) and Website B is "Forma X1" (saved_resource(1).html). Both sites were tested in the 800px review frame with real clicks.

**Website A**
- Its large, detailed printer has a curved banner that hangs naturally.
- The print is so washed out that the pink, yellow and cyan barely show.
- Every control works: drag, the ± and scroll zoom, auto-rotate, Studio and Wireframe, the Isometric, Front and Side cameras, Reset, Expand and the print-head hotspot. The spec tabs, application dialogs and contact form work too.
- Its spec tab lists 13.6k triangles.

**Website B**
- Its isometric printer sits centered in a card, with a vivid cyan, yellow and pink banner and a coral stripe.
- Every control works: three accents (Coral, Cobalt, Graphite), three banner designs (Spectrum, Ocean, Monochrome), wireframe, grid, the camera menu, auto-rotate, Reset, Expand, Save to My collection, and the license, about and quick-start dialogs.
- Its specs list 5,282 triangles.
- Weak point: the Side view shows the banner is a flat sheet, not curved.

**Tie, so left out of the reasons:** both download buttons are blocked in the review frame, and both still show a false "downloaded" or "ready" message.

Written for: the task reviewers. Each reason is 60 words, in third person, with a different opening from the last task.

Aesthetics: Website B
```
Website B is better because its isometric printer sits centered in a soft grey card, and the banner carries a vivid cyan, yellow and pink gradient under white MAKE IT BIG lettering, with a coral stripe running along the body. Website A's printer is larger and its banner curves nicely, but the print is so pale it reads almost white.
```

Functionality: Website B
```
Website B is stronger because its controls change the model: Coral, Cobalt and Graphite recolor the accent stripe, Spectrum, Ocean and Monochrome swap banner prints, and the camera menu snaps to Isometric, Front or Side. Saving adds it to My collection. Website A's views, zoom and hotspot work, but its banner gradient barely shows the requested pink, yellow and cyan.
```

Overall: Website B
```
Website B is the better overall choice. Website A's curved banner hangs more naturally, and Website B's banner shows as a flat sheet in Side view. Still, Website B's vivid pink, yellow and cyan print, centered isometric framing, lighter 5,282-triangle model against Website A's 13.6k, and working accent and banner options clearly outweigh that one advantage for a hero section.
```

content.text:
Website A wins all three for 6253775. Website A is "Crease" (saved_resource.html) and Website B is "Sixer" (saved_resource(1).html).

**Website A**
- Plays a full two-innings match:
  - You bat first, then a "Change of Ends" screen sets the target ("Australia need 15 runs to win").
  - You then bowl with Pace, Spin or Yorker until a result like "India win by 6 runs".
  - A final card shows both teams' scores, and "Your stats" updates.
- Batting has three shots, and at the sweet spot Defend scores 2, Drive 4 and Loft 6. Bad timing on a Loft can get you caught or bowled.
- ODI switches to 50 overs.

**Website B**
- Batting and bowling are separate single innings against a fixed target: 141 in T20, 281 in ODI. There's one swing key plus aiming.
- Timing works: a perfect swing hits "SIX APPEAL!", and the chase was won at 144/0 in 4.1 overs.
- Its "View scorecard" button opens your overall personal stats, not a scorecard for the match.
- The floodlit night stadium looks good, but the bowler figure covers the small caption above every result headline.

Neither game showed errors or got stuck during play.

Written for: the task reviewers. This follows the updated prompt.md: the whole answer in one code block, 60+ words per reason (68, 71 and 63), and nothing about how the sites were checked.

```
Aesthetics: Website A
Website A is the stronger-looking game. Its scoreboard shows team flags, overs and run rate, the This Over strip colors each four and wicket, and the fielders switch to the bowling team's colors after the break. The Change of Ends screen and final card with both flags feel polished. Website B's floodlit night stadium looks great, but the bowler figure sits on top of the small caption above its result headlines.

Functionality: Website A
Website A wins on gameplay because it plays a full match. The player bats first, the Change of Ends screen sets a real target, then the player bowls with Pace, Spin or Yorker until a result like India win by 6 runs appears and Your stats updates. Batting offers Defend, Drive and Loft for different runs. Website B keeps batting and bowling as separate single innings against a fixed 141 target.

Overall: Website A
Website A is the better all-around experience. Website B has the flashier look, with floodlights and huge SIX APPEAL! headlines, and its swing timing feels good. Still, Website A gives a complete cricket match where batting and bowling connect, a real target carries over, and the final card shows both teams' scores, so there is more reason to keep playing one more match.
```

Website B wins Overall. For Satisfaction I'm calling it a tie ("Both are good"), because both edits deliver both requested buttons and both work. Website A is the first wrapper (saved_resource.html) and Website B is the second (saved_resource(1).html).

**Why this task is tricky:**
- It asks only two questions, Satisfaction and Overall, instead of three.
- Each tab is a split screen with "Before Edit" on the left and "After Edit" on the right, and only the right side counts.
- The "before" page is identical in both, so the edit is the only difference.

**What each edit does:**
- **Website A:**
  - A "Play scroll tour" card floats in the corner. It scrolls the page top to bottom in about 75 seconds, with a progress bar, Pause, Stop and Esc, and a mouse-wheel scroll pauses it.
  - At the end the card turns into "Back to top", and the footer also has a labeled "Back to top" button. Both return to the top.
  - The card never goes away. At the bottom of the page it partly covers the footer's "Back to top" button at both 1000px and 1200px, and at 1000px it also covers the "Cookies" link.
- **Website B:**
  - A "Watch the full experience" button sits under the hero buttons. The tour stops briefly at each section, and a floating panel with a percentage, Pause and End appears only while the tour runs.
  - A new "Run complete // 100%" card at the bottom has a large "Go to top" button, and it works.
  - Minor quirks, left out of the reasons: that card says "Run complete" even when nobody ran the tour, and at 1000px wide the start button is just below the first screen.

Written for: the task reviewers. Third person, verdict first, every reason over 60 words (80 and 84), with different openings from the cricket task.

```
Satisfaction: Both are good
Website A and Website B both do what was asked, so both are good here. Website A puts a Play scroll tour button in the corner that rolls the page all the way down with a progress bar, pause and stop, then turns into a Back to top button at the end. Website B's Watch the full experience button scrolls down section by section, and its footer has a big Go to top button that brings the page right back up.

Overall: Website B
Website B comes out ahead overall. Website A's corner tour card is handy because it's always in reach, but it stays pinned over the page the whole time, and at the bottom it partly covers the footer's own Back to top button, which looks messy. Website B keeps its tour button under the hero buttons, pauses a beat at each section so the animations get their moment, and finishes on a clean Run complete card with a wide Go to top button.
```

If you'd rather not submit a tie for Satisfaction, Website B is the next most defensible pick. I can write that reason instead.

The bundles get rebuilt, so the minified names all change. Compare aria-labels, `children:"..."` strings and CSS class names instead of doing a line diff.
- **Pane size:** each After pane is only about 480–680px wide and about 630px tall inside the 800px task frame, so sites switch to their mobile layout. Floating widgets cover more content there. Test there with real mouse input, as in [[review-test-method]].

**Why:** the user said this task type is tricky. It's easy to judge the wrong pane or miss that only the edit differs.

**How to apply:** for each side, check that every part of the request exists and works in the After pane. Then compare how cleanly each edit fits into the page.

Here are the steps that didn't move a verdict or a reason in the tasks so far, so I'll skip them or keep them very short from now on.

**Not worth doing**
- **Download tests** (GLB, PNG, CSV, ZIP). The review frame blocks every download, even when the site says "downloaded", so the result can never be used. You suspected this already, and the tests confirmed it.
- **Phone-width screenshots (390px).** Reviewers struck a phone claim on 6264396 because it couldn't be confirmed from the pages. The 800px review frame matters; a phone does not.
- **Timing and speed numbers.** Tour durations, scroll speeds and how fast animations play all depend on the machine. On Website B's tour my headless browser ran at about half speed, so those numbers aren't usable evidence.
- **Console warnings.** Notices like "THREE.Clock deprecated" or a missing favicon never affected what a reviewer sees.
- **The automatic overlap scanner.** It flagged decorative shapes and missed the real overlap on the fish card. Looking at close-up screenshots worked better.
- **Flaws that only appear at one width.** These can't be used, so measuring several widths is only worth it to confirm a flaw shows at all of them.

**Keep, but shorten**
- **The full 1440px pass.** It's useful for a first look and the aesthetics call, but the 1000×800 review-frame pass is the one that counts.
- **Opening every footer, legal and "About" dialog.** One quick sweep to catch dead buttons is enough, since reviewers do flag those.
- **Reading the site's code.** Decoding and comparing the before/after source on the editing task was very useful. Reading game or geometry logic in depth mostly just helped my test scripts and rarely changed a verdict.
- **Playing games all the way through.** Play the core loop once per mode. On the cricket task, one full match was enough to show that Website A had two connected innings and Website B didn't.

**Most useful**
- Checking each point of the request against what the site actually does.
- Real mouse clicks and hovers inside the 800px review frame.
- Hovering every tooltip or bubble.
- Close-up screenshots of every gallery or card item.
- Naming dead controls exactly.
- On editing tasks, comparing only the After pane against the shared Before page.

input.content:
# UI Berry: Website Preference Tasks

## 1. What I Provide
- A **Task ID**. The folder with that name holds the task HTML (instructions and the User request) and the saved files for Website A and Website B. Sometimes they come zipped.
- Screenshots of both websites (optional, and often cut off).
- Reviewer feedback from earlier tasks in `Prompt/Feedback.md`. Read it before every task.

When a new Task ID comes in, work only from that folder. Never reuse content from a previous task.

---

## 2. Task Types

### Type 1: Aesthetics / Functionality / Overall
Three independent picks. Each one is **A is better / B is better / Both are good / Both are bad**.
- **Aesthetics:** visual quality only (layout, composition, typography, color, polish, spacing, visual defects). Ignore whether controls work.
- **Functionality:** behavior and prompt-following only. Does the requested content render, and do the links, buttons, controls, navigation and interactions work? Ignore polish unless broken rendering blocks the check.
- **Overall:** the complete experience, weighing looks and function together. It doesn't have to match the other two picks.

### Type 2: Editing A/B Preference (Before / After)
Two independent picks: **Satisfaction** and **Overall**.
- Each tab (Website A, Website B) shows a split screen with **Before Edit** on the left and **After Edit** on the right. Judge the **After Edit** side. The Before page is usually the same for both.
- **Satisfaction:** does the After site do what the edit request asked? Are the requested parts there, and do they work? Ignore polish unless it blocks use.
- **Overall:** the **whole After website**, not just the new feature. That means the hero section, images, navigation bar, every section, all buttons, the requested feature, and how it all looks and works together.

### Which file is which
In the task HTML, the first iframe sits in the "Website A" tab and the second in the "Website B" tab. Usually Website A is `saved_resource.html` and Website B is `saved_resource(1).html`. For editing tasks, open each of those two wrapper files to find its Before and After files.

A site that fails to load, freezes or can't be inspected counts as a **functionality failure**.

---

## 3. How to Evaluate

### 3.1 Start with the request
Read the User request and turn it into a checklist of every concrete requirement:
- the elements and content asked for
- colors and style
- modes (for example T20 and ODI, batting and bowling)
- behaviors (hover, scroll, export)
- limits (for example "just one page, no extra views")

Every requirement gets checked on both websites.

### 3.2 Test the way the reviewer does
Reviewers use each site inside the task page: a frame about **1000px wide and 800px tall**. Editing panes are only about **480–680px wide**. Test there, with real mouse clicks, hovers and key presses.
- Click **every** button, tab, filter, toggle, card, tile, menu item and footer link, and note what each one does. Note the ones that do nothing.
- Make sure menu items and buttons are clickable across their whole area, not just one spot.
- Hover **every** tooltip, bubble and hotspot.
- Open **every** gallery or collection item and look at each card up close for overlaps, cut-off text and broken labels.
- On forms, try blank input and bad input.
- On games and tools, run the core loop once in **each requested mode**.
- Take one full-size look for the overall visual impression.

### 3.3 What counts as evidence
- **Only what a reviewer sees in normal use** within a minute or two of playing or clicking. If a state takes a long play-through (a final match result, a later stage), describe it through what's visible on the page instead: the scoreboard, the buttons, the rules text, the target shown.
- **Never use as evidence:**
  - whether a file download works (downloads are blocked in the review frame; a menu item that can't be clicked is still a valid point)
  - phone or mobile layout
  - timing or speed numbers
  - console messages
  - flaws that only show at one window size
- **A feature both sites have is never a difference.** Before crediting one site, confirm the other doesn't have it too, and call shared features shared.
- **Before calling something an advantage, look at it again.** If it could just as easily be read as a flaw, leave it out.
- **Don't over-claim.** Describe only what was actually shown on the page.

### 3.4 What to check under each lens

**Aesthetics**
- Match to the requested look: colors, style and shape (for example a pink, yellow and cyan banner, a soft rounded star, brand colors).
- The main visual (hero, logo, model, chart, character), with a specific detail of how it's drawn. Example: "a crate drawn as a flat dark green silhouette with only the carrot in color".
- Layout and spacing: crowded areas, alignment, balance, empty space.
- Typography and readability: text over photos, pale labels fading into the background, contrast.
- Visible defects: overlaps (for example "the seventh fish overlaps its text"), cut-off text, wrong labels, elements covering other content.
- Consistency and polish across sections, cards and icons.

**Functionality**
- Each item on the request checklist: present, and does it work?
- Each control named with its result (for example "the Earnings chip filters the bubbles", "the ODI card switches to 50 overs").
- Dead or half-working controls named exactly (for example "code tiles do nothing on click", "the portfolio and settings buttons lead nowhere").
- Options counted (for example "three backgrounds and an SVG-only download", "five body colors").
- Working features only one site has (for example "only Website B opens each logo in a larger preview").
- Navigation: menu links, tabs and pages actually open.
- Forms: whether they reject blank or invalid input.
- Modes and saved state: requested modes switch, saves persist, reset works.
- Following the request's limits: extra pages or views the request said not to add.
- **Visual details never go in Functionality** (for example a pale banner or a crowded layout).

**Satisfaction (editing tasks)**
- Each requested change is in the After site, works with a real click, and does the whole job. For example, it scrolls all the way to the bottom, and the go-to-top button at the bottom takes the page back to the top.
- Ignore polish unless it blocks use.

**Overall**
- Cover the whole site: hero, images, navigation bar, sections, all buttons, and the requested features.
- Weigh at least one visual point against at least one behavior point.
- If both sites are strong and differ only in small drawbacks, choose **Both are good**. Pick a side only for a clear, meaningful difference. Choose **Both are bad** when both fail the core request.

### 3.5 Decision rules
- Each question is judged on its own. Overall can differ from the others.
- Decide by the **biggest, most visible difference in that lens**, not by counting small nitpicks.
- Ties are allowed, and they're correct when the sites really are even.
- The option picked in the form must match what the reason says.

---

## 4. How to Write Each Reason

### 4.1 Opening sentence (mandatory)
The first sentence states the pick, naming the websites **in full**:
- Website A is better because...
- Website A is the best option because...
- Website A is preferred...
- Website A is stronger...
- For ties: **Both Website A and Website B are good because...** or **Both Website A and Website B are bad because...**

The word "because" is optional. Never use "A" or "B" alone, "Candidate 1/2", "Website 1/2", or a bare "Website is...". **Name both Website A and Website B in full in every reason.**

### 4.2 Body
- **Aesthetics:** concrete visual details of the winner (colors, shapes, what the main visual looks like), then the other site's specific visual problem. No "less personality" or "looks nicer" without saying what's on the screen.
- **Functionality:** control and result, options counted, dead controls named. Shared features are stated as shared. No visual details. Never "fewer controls" or "more limited" without listing exactly what's missing.
- **Satisfaction:** each requested part, and that it works (or exactly how it fails).
- **Overall:** write it **last**. Cover the whole site, weigh one visual point against one behavior point, and finish with a clear comparison. Don't copy the Functionality reason, and don't hedge in a way that blurs which side wins.
- **Ties:** give each site's main strength, then say why its small drawbacks don't change the verdict.

### 4.3 Voice and style
- **Third person only.** No "I", "me", "my", "we" or "my pick". Avoid "you" too; say "users", "visitors" or "the player".
- **Native, everyday spoken American English** that doesn't sound AI-written. Keep it simple, the way a person talks.
- Clear for **technical and non-technical readers alike**. Use plain words, and skip jargon (WebGL, GLB, PBR, triangle counts) unless the request itself uses those terms.
- No em dashes, and no filler words like "seamless", "elevate" or "robust".
- Proofread: complete sentences, no comma splices, a period at the end, correct names of on-page labels.
- **Change the sentence style for every new task** so openings and rhythm differ from the previous task.
- **Don't mention how the sites were checked** ("I clicked", "in testing", "after checking").
- Only facts confirmed on the pages.

### 4.4 Length
- **60+ words per reason, and never under 40.** Count the words in each field before submitting.

---

## 5. Answer Format
Write the whole result in **one code block**.

Aesthetics / Functionality / Overall tasks:
```
Aesthetics: Website B
Reason sentences

Functionality: Website A
Reason sentences

Overall: Website A
Reason sentences
```

Editing tasks:
```
Satisfaction: Both are good
Reason sentences

Overall: Website B
Reason sentences
```

---

## 6. Final Checklist (before submitting)
- [ ] Every requirement in the User request was checked on both websites.
- [ ] Each reason opens with the verdict (winner or tie), with Website A and Website B named in full.
- [ ] Both websites are named in every reason.
- [ ] Third person throughout. No "I", "me", "my" or "you".
- [ ] Aesthetics has only visual points; Functionality has only behavior points.
- [ ] Controls are named with their results, options are counted, dead controls are named.
- [ ] No feature both sites share is used as a difference.
- [ ] Nothing described as an advantage could be read as a flaw.
- [ ] Every claim is something a reviewer can see in normal use (no downloads, phone layouts, timing or long end states).
- [ ] Overall was written last, covers the whole site, and weighs a visual point against a behavior point.
- [ ] Tie options are used when both sites are about equally good or bad.
- [ ] 60+ words per reason (never under 40), counted.
- [ ] Grammar checked, sentence style changed from the last task, no testing steps mentioned.
- [ ] The pick in the form matches the pick in the reason.

---

## 7. Lessons from Reviewer Feedback
| Task | What went wrong | Rule now |
|---|---|---|
| 6250482 | "Less personality" with no evidence; "more limited" with no list | Describe exactly what's on screen; list the exact options and dead controls |
| 6257531 | "Website is the better choice" with no letter | Name Website A and Website B in full in every reason |
| 6261407 | Talked about general layout and missed the real differences | Look for unique working features and visible overlaps on every item |
| 6264396 | First person; a phone claim that couldn't be confirmed | Third person only; no phone claims; name each control and its result |
| 6255409 | First person; verdict not stated first | Open with the verdict sentence |
| 6250470 | Said downloads worked when menu items weren't fully clickable; "fewer controls" | Never claim downloads; check click areas; name exactly what's missing |
| 6251496 / 6243305 | Overall copied Functionality; a reason had only 35 words | Write Overall last with one point from each lens; count words |
| 6241898 | Credited one site with camera views both had; a visual point in Functionality; a flaw called an advantage | Check that each control is really unique; keep the lenses separate; double-check every advantage |
| 6265185 | Typos and thin details | Proofread; add specific supporting details |
| 6253775 | Described end-of-match states the reviewer never reached | Use only what's visible in normal use; describe longer flows through what's on the page |
| 6260728 | Tie reason didn't open with the tie; wrong option picked in the form; Overall only covered the new buttons | Open with "Both Website A and Website B are good because..."; check the form pick; Overall covers the whole site; small drawbacks on two strong sites mean Both are good |

Reviewers use each site inside the task page: a frame about **1000px wide and 800px tall**. Editing panes are only about **480–680px wide**. Test there, with real mouse clicks, hovers and key presses.
- Click **every** button, tab, filter, toggle, card, tile, menu item and footer link, and note what each one does. Note the ones that do nothing.
- Make sure menu items and buttons are clickable across their whole area, not just one spot.
- Hover **every** tooltip, bubble and hotspot.
- Open **every** gallery or collection item and look at each card up close for overlaps, cut-off text and broken labels.
- On forms, try blank input and bad input.
- On games and tools, run the core loop once in **each requested mode**.
- Take one full-size look for the overall visual impression.

### 3.3 What counts as evidence
- **Only what a reviewer sees in normal use** within a minute or two of playing or clicking. If a state takes a long play-through (a final match result, a later stage), describe it through what's visible on the page instead: the scoreboard, the buttons, the rules text, the target shown.
- **Never use as evidence:**
  - whether a file download works (downloads are blocked in the review frame; a menu item that can't be clicked is still a valid point)
  - phone or mobile layout
  - timing or speed numbers
  - console messages
  - flaws that only show at one window size
- **A feature both sites have is never a difference.** Before crediting one site, confirm the other doesn't have it too, and call shared features shared.
- **Before calling something an advantage, look at it again.** If it could just as easily be read as a flaw, leave it out.
- **Don't over-claim.** Describe only what was actually shown on the page.

### 3.4 What to check under each lens

**Aesthetics**
- Match to the requested look: colors, style and shape (for example a pink, yellow and cyan banner, a soft rounded star, brand colors).
- The main visual (hero, logo, model, chart, character), with a specific detail of how it's drawn. Example: "a crate drawn as a flat dark green silhouette with only the carrot in color".
- Layout and spacing: crowded areas, alignment, balance, empty space.
- Typography and readability: text over photos, pale labels fading into the background, contrast.
- Visible defects: overlaps (for example "the seventh fish overlaps its text"), cut-off text, wrong labels, elements covering other content.
- Consistency and polish across sections, cards and icons.

**Functionality**
- Each item on the request checklist: present, and does it work?
- Each control named with its result (for example "the Earnings chip filters the bubbles", "the ODI card switches to 50 overs").
- Dead or half-working controls named exactly (for example "code tiles do nothing on click", "the portfolio and settings buttons lead nowhere").
- Options counted (for example "three backgrounds and an SVG-only download", "five body colors").
- Working features only one site has (for example "only Website B opens each logo in a larger preview").
- Navigation: menu links, tabs and pages actually open.
- Forms: whether they reject blank or invalid input.
- Modes and saved state: requested modes switch, saves persist, reset works.
- Following the request's limits: extra pages or views the request said not to add.
- **Visual details never go in Functionality** (for example a pale banner or a crowded layout).

**Satisfaction (editing tasks)**
- Each requested change is in the After site, works with a real click, and does the whole job. For example, it scrolls all the way to the bottom, and the go-to-top button at the bottom takes the page back to the top.
- Ignore polish unless it blocks use.

- Cover the whole site: hero, images, navigation bar, sections, all buttons, and the requested features.

- If both sites are strong and differ only in small drawbacks, choose **Both are good**. Pick a side only for a clear, meaningful difference. Choose **Both are bad** when both fail the core request.

### 3.5 Decision rules
- Each question is judged on its own. Overall can differ from the others.
- Decide by the **biggest, most visible difference in that lens**, not by counting small nitpicks.
- Ties are allowed, and they're correct when the sites really are even.
- The option picked in the form must match what the reason says.

## 4. How to Write Each Reason

### 4.1 Opening sentence (mandatory)
The first sentence states the pick, naming the websites **in full**:
- Website A is better because...
- Website A is the best option because...
- Website A is preferred...
- Website A is stronger...

The word "because" is optional. Never use "A" or "B" alone, "Candidate 1/2", "Website 1/2", or a bare "Website is...". **Name both Website A and Website B in full in every reason.**

### 4.2 Body
- **Aesthetics:** concrete visual details of the winner (colors, shapes, what the main visual looks like), then the other site's specific visual problem. No "less personality" or "looks nicer" without saying what's on the screen.

### 4.3 Voice and style
- **Third person only.** No "I", "me", "my", "we" or "my pick". Avoid "you" too; say "users", "visitors" or "the player".
- **Native, everyday spoken American English** that doesn't sound AI-written. Keep it simple, the way a person talks.

- **Don't mention how the sites were checked** ("I clicked", "in testing", "after checking").

Aesthetics: Website B

Functionality: Website A
Reason sentences

Overall: Website A

name: editing-task-format
description: "How \"Editing A/B Preference\" UI Berry tasks are structured (before/after wrappers, Satisfaction + Overall questions) and how to analyze them"
metadata:

Some UI Berry tasks are "Editing A/B Preference" rather than Aesthetics/Functionality/Overall. First seen on task 6260728 (2026-10-16).

- **Two questions only:** Satisfaction (does the edit fulfill the request; ignore polish unless it blocks use) and Overall (function plus looks). The options are "A is better / B is better / Both are good / Both are bad". Write "Satisfaction: …" and "Overall: …" in the same code-block format as [[follow-feedback-md]].
- **Wrappers:** the Website A and Website B tabs each load a small wrapper (saved_resource.html and saved_resource(1).html). Each wrapper shows the request banner and two side-by-side panes, "Before Edit" and "After Edit". Only the After pane is judged. On 6260728, A was before (2) / after (3) and B was before (4) / after (5). Always confirm this from the wrapper's iframe src values.
- **The "before" page is usually identical in both,** so the edit is the only difference.
- **Reading the code:** the big (~25MB) saved pages have a header comment `saved from url=(N)data:text/html;base64,...` that holds the original page source. Decode it and compare before/after. The bundles get rebuilt, so the minified names all change. Compare aria-labels, `children:"..."` strings and CSS class names instead of doing a line diff.
- **Pane size:** each After pane is only about 480–680px wide and about 630px tall inside the 800px task frame, so sites switch to their mobile layout. Floating widgets cover more content there. Test there with real mouse input, as in [[review-test-method]].

**Why:** the user said this task type is tricky. It's easy to judge the wrong pane or miss that only the edit differs.

**How to apply:** for each side, check that every part of the request exists and works in the After pane. Then compare how cleanly each edit fits into the page.

Written for: you and the AI sessions that will run future UI Berry tasks.

I rewrote [prompt.md](Prompt/prompt.md) as one rulebook covering every lesson in the feedback, including the four newest entries on my own answers. The old version is still in prompt-original.md, which matches it exactly.

**What's new in it:**
- **Task types:** it covers both formats, Aesthetics/Functionality/Overall and Editing (Satisfaction/Overall). For Editing tasks it says to judge the After Edit side, and that Overall covers the whole site: hero, images, navigation bar and all buttons.
- **How to test:** test the way reviewers do, inside an 800px-tall frame with real clicks. Click every control and check its whole click area, hover every bubble, and look at every gallery card up close.
- **Evidence rules:** only claim what a reviewer sees in normal use. Never claim downloads, phone layouts, timing numbers, or results that take a long play-through. Never count a feature both sites share. Double-check every "advantage".
- **What to check under each lens:** a checklist for Aesthetics, Functionality, Satisfaction and Overall, with examples taken from the feedback. Visual points never go in Functionality.
- **When to choose a tie:** if both sites are strong and differ only in small drawbacks, the answer is "Both are good". Pick a side only for a clear, meaningful difference.
- **Writing pattern:**
  - The first sentence states the verdict, ties included ("Both Website A and Website B are good because...").
  - Third person, with no "I" and no "you", and plain words for non-technical readers.
  - Overall is written last and weighs a visual point against a behavior point.
  - At least 60 words per reason, proofread, with a new sentence style for each task.
- **Final checklist:** 14 checks to run before submitting, including that the option picked in the form matches the reason.
- **Lessons table:** one row per reviewed task, showing what went wrong and the rule now.

My memory now points to prompt.md as the rulebook, so new sessions will follow it and check Feedback.md for newer notes. When feedback comes in on future tasks, I'll add it to the lessons table.

### 3.6 Steps to skip or keep short
These have never changed a verdict or a reason, so don't spend time on them.

**Skip:**
- **Testing file downloads** (GLB, PNG, SVG, CSV, ZIP). They're blocked in the review frame, and a "downloaded" message proves nothing. Only check that the download button or menu item can be clicked.
- **Phone or mobile screenshots.** Reviewers can't confirm phone claims. The 800px review frame is what matters.
- **Measuring timing or speed** (scroll duration, animation speed, frame rate). The numbers change from machine to machine.
- **Reading console warnings** ("deprecated" notices, a missing favicon). Reviewers never see them.
- **Automatic overlap scanners.** They flag decorative shapes and miss real overlaps. Look at close-up screenshots instead.
- **Hunting for flaws at many window sizes.** A flaw that shows at only one width can't be used.

**Keep short:**
- **The full-size view:** one look for the overall visual impression. The review-frame check is the one that counts.
- **Footer, legal and "About" links:** one quick pass to catch dead links. No need to read every dialog.
- **Reading the site's code:** only when it saves time. For example, decoding and comparing the Before/After source on editing tasks shows exactly what changed. Don't study game or 3D logic in depth.
- **Games:** play the core loop once in each requested mode. No need to play to the end. Describe longer flows through what's visible on the page (see 3.3).

### Task: 6253775
## Answers:
# Aesthetics: Website A
Website A is the stronger-looking game. Its scoreboard shows team flags, overs and run rate, the This Over strip colors each four and wicket, and the fielders switch to the bowling team's colors after the break. The Change of Ends screen and final card with both flags feel polished. Website B's floodlit night stadium looks great, but the bowler figure sits on top of the small caption above its result headlines.

# Functionality: Website A
Website A wins on gameplay because it plays a full match. The player bats first, the Change of Ends screen sets a real target, then the player bowls with Pace, Spin or Yorker until a result like India win by 6 runs appears and Your stats updates. Batting offers Defend, Drive and Loft for different runs. Website B keeps batting and bowling as separate single innings against a fixed 141 target.

# Overall: Website A
Website A is the better all-around experience. Website B has the flashier look, with floodlights and huge SIX APPEAL! headlines, and its swing timing feels good. Still, Website A gives a complete cricket match where batting and bowling connect, a real target carries over, and the final card shows both teams' scores, so there is more reason to keep playing one more match.

## Feedback: 
The three picks for Website A were right, and the contrast with Website B's fixed target of 141 was the right basis for functionality and overall. The writeups went past the evidence by describing a finished result, a target carried to the end, a change of ends, and fielder colors that were not shown, while the board stayed at 0 with an open target. I kept your choices and rewrote the reasons around the scoreboard, the shot and delivery choices, the role-switch rules, and Website B's unchanged 20-over chase.

### Task: 6260728
## Answers:
# Satisfaction: Both are good
Website A and Website B both do what was asked, so both are good here. Website A puts a Play scroll tour button in the corner that rolls the page all the way down with a progress bar, pause and stop, then turns into a Back to top button at the end. Website B's Watch the full experience button scrolls down section by section, and its footer has a big Go to top button that brings the page right back up.

# Overall: Website B
Website B comes out ahead overall. Website A's corner tour card is handy because it's always in reach, but it stays pinned over the page the whole time, and at the bottom it partly covers the footer's own Back to top button, which looks messy. Website B keeps its tour button under the hero buttons, pauses a beat at each section so the animations get their moment, and finishes on a clean Run complete card with a wide Go to top button.

## Feedback:
Your Satisfaction reason is correct, but you must start with the winner/tied sentence, and you chose Both are bad even though you indicated that both are good. In the overall, you indicated some aspect somewhat ambiguos and you based your overall reason solely on the new buttons, whereas you should have evaluated everything, aesthetics and functionality alike. There were new hero sections, new images, button functionalities and a navigation bar, yet you didnt mention any of them. Both have some drawbacks, but overall they are very good solutions, therefore both are good would be the best conclusion.
Score: 2.

## Answers:
# Aesthetics: Both are good
Both Website A and Website B are good because each one gives the classic game a clean, finished look. Website A sets a dark green board inside a soft cream page, with a light green snake, an orange fruit and a huge score number on the side. Website B goes fully dark with a giant SNAKE headline, a glowing lime snake and a red apple. Website B's grey helper text is a little faint, and Website A's small captions are tiny, but those are small things.

# Functionality: Both are good
Both Website A and Website B are good because the full snake game works the same way on each. Every piece of food adds 10 points and makes the snake one piece longer, hitting a wall ends the round, Space pauses, the Restart button starts over, and Chill, Classic and Fast change the speed. The best score stays saved after a reload on both. Website A adds clickable arrow buttons and a How to play window, while Website B lets players steer by dragging across the board.

# Overall: Both are good
Both Website A and Website B are good overall, because each page is built around a working snake game with nothing broken or missing. Website A wraps it in a bright cream layout with a How to play window, a sound switch and a game over card that calls out a new personal best. Website B gives the same game a darker arcade feel, with a bold SNAKE headline and numbered difficulty and how-to-play sections. Website B's arrow icons are only hints, not buttons, but that small gap doesn't change the call.

## Answers:
# Aesthetics: Both are good
Both Website A and Website B are good because each one shows a convincing 3D machine in a polished layout. Website A puts a dark engine cutaway on a near-black page, with a white spark plug, a finned cylinder and labeled valve, piston and crankshaft. Website B shows a silver gearbox with orange bearing rings on a clean light grid, framed by a tidy design-tool sidebar. Website B's side panels pack in a lot of small text, but that doesn't change the call.

# Functionality: Both are good
Both Website A and Website B are good because their 3D models really work and explain the machine. On Website A, Play runs the full 720-degree cycle, the Intake, Compression, Power and Exhaust buttons move the piston and rewrite the step text, Exploded lifts the head off, and picking Crankshaft lights it up in the model. On Website B, Exploded pulls the gearbox apart with a Separation slider, the eye icons hide the housing, the simulation spins the gears, and raising input speed to 1800 rpm changes the output to 600 rpm.

# Overall: Both are good
Both Website A and Website B are good overall, since each one is a complete, well-built page around its machine. Website A pairs its moody engine cutaway with a step-by-step cycle panel, a parts section and a specs table, which makes the working idea easy to follow. Website B feels like a real design tool, with camera views, a properties panel, a documentation tab and Share and Export windows. Website A explains a bit more, Website B lets people tinker a bit more, and neither one has a real weak spot.

content.text:
I re-checked task 3979081 more carefully, and the verdict stays at "Both are good" for all three. Every claim in my earlier reasons held up, and the closer look turned up no real flaw on either site.

**What I checked this time:**
- **Website A, motion:** the piston and crank visibly move during Play. The step text switches from Intake to Compression right at 180°, and clicking the crank slider at 75% jumps to Exhaust at 543°.
- **Website A, rest of the page:** speed choices of 0.5×, 1.5× and 2× work. The full page renders cleanly in the review frame: the four-stroke cards, a parts list where each part opens a line drawing and a "Find it in the model" link, the specs table, and the footer. The large gaps in my earlier captures were just animations that hadn't finished playing.
- **Website B, viewer:** the gears turn during the simulation, and with the housing hidden the inner gear pair shows clearly. Choosing Brushed brass recolors the gears, Motion paths draws dashed orbit rings, and "Watch it work" on the Overview tab starts the simulation.
- **Website B, pages and dialogs:** the Documentation tab has Specifications, Operating principle and Assembly guide sections, and the Share, Export, settings and version dialogs all open.

The only things I found are cosmetic and too small to change a verdict:
- Website B's hidden-housing view leaves the bolts floating in the air, because the bolts are a separate part you can hide on their own.
- Website B's side panels are crowded with small text.

I added the newly confirmed details to make the reasons stronger.

Written for: the task reviewers.

```
Aesthetics: Both are good
Both Website A and Website B are good because each one gives its machine a realistic, carefully lit 3D look. Website A shows a dark engine cutaway on a near-black page, with a white spark plug, finned cylinder walls and lime labels, and its parts section adds neat line drawings. Website B shows a silver helical gearbox with orange bearing rings on a light grid inside a clean design-tool layout. Website B's side panels are packed with small text, but that doesn't change the call.

Functionality: Both are good
Both Website A and Website B are good because every main control works. On Website A, Play runs the full 720-degree cycle, the Intake, Compression, Power and Exhaust buttons move the piston and rewrite the step text, the crank slider and the 0.5x to 2x speeds work, and Exploded lifts the head off. On Website B, Exploded spreads the parts with a Separation slider, the eye icons hide the housing, the simulation spins the gears, Brushed brass recolors them, and a higher input speed raises the output speed.

Overall: Both are good
Both Website A and Website B are good overall, since each one is a complete, well-built page about its machine. Website A walks through the engine with a stroke-by-stroke panel, a parts list with drawings and a specs table, so the working idea is easy to follow. Website B works like a real design tool, with camera views, motion paths, a documentation tab and Share and Export windows. Website A explains a bit more, Website B lets people tinker a bit more, and neither one has a real weak spot.
```

# Aesthetics: Both are good
Website A and Website B each give the classic game a clean finished look and are therefore good. Website A places a dark green board in a light cream page and adds a light green snake, a fruit, and a huge score number on the side. Website B goes completely dark with a huge SNAKE headline, a glowing lime snake and a red apple. Website A’s and Website B’s gray helper text is faint and A’s small captions are tiny, but that is a minor issue.

Website A and Website B are both good because the full snake game works the same on both. Every piece of food adds 10 points and makes the snake one piece longer, hitting a wall ends the round, Space pauses, the Restart button resets the game, and the options Chill, Classic and Fast change the game speed.
The best score is saved upon reload for both. Website A adds a How to play window and arrow buttons, while Website B allows steering by dragging.

# Overall: Both are good
Website A and Website B are both good, as each features a page with a functioning snake game with no broken elements. Website A has a bright, cream-colored background with a How to Play window, sound toggle, and Game Over card that displays the new personal best. Website B gives the same game with a darker, more arcade-style background with a large header that says SNAKE and numbered difficulty and how to play sections. The arrow icons on Website B are more hints than controls, but that doesn't change the outcome.

The bare-letter warning is a false positive: it matched the "A and" inside "Website A and Website B". All other checks pass, with straight apostrophes only, no stiff connecting words, and 88–96 words per reason.

All three answers for task 1210318 are "Both are good". Website A is "Sendly" (saved_resource.html) and Website B is "Sendflow" (saved_resource(1).html). Every requested part works on both:
- **Layout:** sidebar, top bar with Start/Stop and a RUNNING/PAUSED status, campaign switcher, notifications and profile.
- **Dashboard:** stats cards, a live progress bar, the email currently sending and a live activity feed.
- **Campaign builder:** CSV upload, delay, extra subject lines, message templates and a live email preview.
- **Extras:** logs table with search, toasts, dark mode, and frosted glass cards.
- **Backend calls:**
  - Website B calls POST / with FormData, GET /progress, GET /logs and GET /stop right away, then falls back to a preview mode.
  - Website A starts in Demo mode. Once Flask mode is switched on in Settings it makes the same POST /, /progress and /logs calls. I didn't trigger its Stop call in Flask mode, so I didn't claim GET /stop for Website A.

Each site has a few small extras the other lacks, but neither has a real weak spot:
- **Website A:** a settings screen that lists all four endpoints, and an email preview that fills in names from the uploaded CSV.
- **Website B:** separate message template tabs, plus Full preview and Send a test windows.

Written for: the task reviewers.

Aesthetics: Both are good
Both Website A and Website B are good because each one looks like a polished, modern SaaS dashboard with a sidebar, a top bar and soft frosted glass cards. Website A uses a clean light layout with purple buttons and a purple progress bar, and it turns into a deep purple-black dark mode with one switch. Website B starts in a dark green theme with lime buttons and a bright lime progress bar, and it switches to a light mode just as easily. Neither one has a visual problem that stands out.

Functionality: Both are good

Start and Stop sending flip the status between RUNNING and PAUSED with a toast, the progress bar and live activity feed keep updating, and the campaign picker swaps in that campaign's numbers. Uploading a CSV imports the contacts, extra subject lines can be added, and typing a message updates the preview. Both send the campaign form to the backend as FormData and check /progress and /logs, with Website A doing it once Flask mode is turned on in Settings.

Overall: Both are good
Both Website A and Website B are good overall, since each one is a complete, working campaign dashboard that's ready for a Flask backend. Website A stands out with a Demo or Flask switch in Settings that lists the four endpoints, and its email preview fills in names from the uploaded CSV. Website B stands out with a bold dark look, separate message template tabs, and Full preview and Send a test windows. Each one has its own small extras, and neither one has a real weak spot.
```

content.text:
For task 3977933 (show TRX and predict its 2030 price), Aesthetics is a tie and Website A wins Functionality and Overall. Website A is "Tronlens" (saved_resource.html) and Website B is "Tronscope" (saved_resource(1).html). Every control I clicked worked on both sites, inside the review frame.

- **Shared by both:** price chart time-range buttons, hover tooltips on the price and forecast charts, a USD/EUR/GBP currency switch, bear/base/bull scenarios, a watchlist, and methodology and data notes.
- **Only Website A:** the prediction can be adjusted. The growth slider gives a custom 2030 estimate ($1.16 at +42%). The forecast page shows each year, the math behind it, and a Reset to base case button. It also has a candlestick chart view and separate TRON network and methodology pages.
- **Only Website B:** a light/dark mode switch and a 3M range button. Its 2030 prices are fixed at $0.18, $0.85 and $1.65.
- **Why Aesthetics is a tie:** Website A is a clean white and red design, and Website B is dark with a glowing red logo. Both are polished, with no visual flaws.

Written for: the task reviewers. All reasons pass the checks (straight apostrophes, no stiff words, Website A and Website B always in full, 82, 90 and 84 words).

```
Aesthetics: Both are good
Both Website A and Website B are good to look at, and each one turns TRX into a clear, modern finance dashboard. Website A goes with a bright white layout, red accents, a soft red price line and an orange highlight on its 2030 card. Website B goes dark, with a glowing red TRON logo, big white price numbers and a dashed three-line forecast chart. The styles are different, but neither one has crowded spots, cut-off text or anything broken on screen.

Functionality: Website A
Website A is stronger on function because visitors can change its 2030 prediction themselves. Dragging the annual growth slider gives a custom estimate, like $1.16 at +42%, and the 2030 forecast page breaks it down year by year with the math shown and a Reset to base case button. Its price chart also switches between a line and a candlestick view. Both sites have time range buttons, hover prices, a currency switch and bear, base and bull scenarios, but Website B's 2030 numbers stay fixed at $0.18, $0.85 and $1.65.

Overall: Website A
Website A is the better overall pick. Website B has the moodier dark look and a light mode switch, and its single page is easy to scroll through. Website A matches it on polish with a clean white layout, and it goes further where the request matters most: visitors can set their own growth rate to predict the 2030 price, then check each year on a separate forecast page, plus TRON network and methodology pages. That deeper prediction tool gives Website A the edge.
```

---
name: follow-feedback-md
description: For every UI Berry website-comparison task, follow Prompt/prompt.md (the consolidated rulebook) and check Prompt/Feedback.md for new reviewer notes
metadata:
  type: feedback
---

`Prompt/prompt.md` is the full rulebook. It covers task types, what to check under each lens, evidence rules, the writing pattern, a final checklist and a lessons table (§7) with one row per reviewed task. On every task, read prompt.md, then scan Feedback.md for new `## Feedback:` entries and fold them into §7 and the rules.

Scores so far (2026-10-22): 3987088=4, 3979081=4, 3988061=4, 1210318=3, 3977933=3, 3978133=4. Lessons that cost the most points:
- **Evidence must be on screen only.** No claims from code or network traffic (1210318: backend-call claims removed). Nothing that depends on saved storage or a reload (3978133). Measure sizes before comparing (3978133: a "tiny sprite" was really the same size).
- **Visible flaws decide picks and break ties.** Broken or missing images are a Functionality failure (3988061). Empty gaps or uneven columns count against Aesthetics, and a status label that doesn't match the real state (like "Live" while paused) is a Functionality bug (1210318: all three ties flipped to Website A).
- **Ties must name one weak spot for each site.** Never write "neither has a weak spot" (3979081).
- **Aesthetics and Overall need rich, concrete detail.** Aim for 80–110 words with specific colors, shapes and labels (3977933: too brief, score 3).
- **Format:** verdict sentence first with both sites named in full, third person, straight apostrophes only, one paragraph per reason, and no "therefore" or other stiff connectors.

**Why:** the user's goal is 5/5 on every task, and each lost point traces back to one of the rules above.

**How to apply:** run the prompt.md §6 checklist before handing over answers. See also [[task-workflow]], [[review-test-method]] and [[editing-task-format]].

Reviewers judge each site inside the task page's iframe. It is 800px tall, roughly 800–1100px wide in a split view, and sandboxed with `allow-scripts allow-same-origin allow-popups allow-popups-to-escape-sandbox allow-forms`. There is no `allow-downloads`.

Lessons from past tasks (6250470, 6261407, 6250482, 6251496, 6264396):
- Chrome blocks every file download inside that iframe ("Download is disallowed… sandboxed"), even when the site shows a success toast. On 6250470 an answer said "both downloads work" and the reviewer marked it wrong. Never use a download as evidence unless it was checked in the frame. Prefer behavior that works there, such as localStorage saves, dialogs and redraws.
- Click with real mouse input (`page.mouse.click`) and check `elementFromPoint`. `element.click()` from script bypasses overlays and hit-testing and hides broken controls.
- Screenshot and look at every gallery or collection item close up. On 6261407 the overlap on the 7th fish card was missed because only the first screen was captured. Text inside SVG badges can be covered by shapes, and automated overlap scans miss it.
- Click every tile, card or code block that looks clickable, and name the dead ones ("code tiles that do nothing on click"). Count the options, for example "three backgrounds, SVG-only download", instead of writing "more limited".
- Back visual claims with concrete evidence, for example "a flat dark green silhouette with only the carrot in color" or "pale labels fade over the yellow photo".
- No phone or mobile claims. Reviewers can't confirm them from the pages (6264396). Prefer flaws that show at every desktop width over ones that only appear at one size.

content.text:
I'm ready for the next task. I went through the six reviews from today (scores 3–4) and updated [prompt.md](Prompt/prompt.md), the final checklist and my memory so these mistakes don't come back.

**Changes to how I evaluate**
- **Only what's on screen.** No claims taken from the code or network traffic. The backend-call claims on 1210318 were removed. No claims that rely on saved storage after a reload either, like the best score on 3978133.
- **Broken images count as a failure.** On 3988061 I suspected Website A's firearm photo might be missing only from the saved files and left it out. The reviewer saw it broken and gave Functionality to Website B. From now on, a missing image counts.
- **Small visible flaws break ties.** On 1210318 the reviewer turned all three ties into Website A wins because of an empty gap under Website B's preview card and a "Live" label still showing while paused. I now check every page for uneven columns, empty gaps and status labels that don't match the real state.
- **Measure before comparing sizes.** On 3978133, Website B's bird looked tiny in a shrunk screenshot but was really about the same size as Website A's.

**Changes to how I write**
- **Every tie names one weak spot for each site.** No more "neither has a weak spot" (3979081).
- **Aesthetics and Overall get as much detail as Functionality.** About 80–110 words, with specific colors, shapes, frames, titles and labels (3977933 was marked too brief).
- **One paragraph per reason, straight apostrophes only.** Curly apostrophes were flagged on three tasks. They seem to come back when the text is edited before submitting, so it's worth checking after any edits.

Send the next Task ID whenever you're ready.

content.text:
Website A wins all three lenses for task 3979206. Website A is "Common" (saved_resource.html) and Website B is "roomly" (saved_resource(1).html). Both load all their images, show appliances down the side and 0:00–23:59 across the top in 15-minute slots, and move between days with bookings for each day.

- **Room-first rule:** both sites enforce it.
  - Website A shows a message with a "Book the room" button.
  - Website B opens the room booking dialog.
- **Overlapping bookings:** both block them with a clear message.
- **Cancelling a room:** both warn that the appliance bookings inside it will be cancelled too.
- **Appliance booking past the room's end time:**
  - Website A refuses it with a clear error.
  - Website B shows a warning in the dialog, but pressing Confirm just closes the window, with nothing saved and no explanation.
- **Short bookings:** Website B's one-hour bars cut off the user name and time range ("Jamie Park 08:00 - 09:...", "Alex Mor... 13:15 - 14:..."). Website A's sample bars all show both in full.
- **Website A's weak spot:** its wide sidebar squeezes the timeline to about six hours at a time. I named this in the reasons, as the reviewers asked.

All checks pass: one paragraph each, straight quotes and apostrophes, no stiff words, about 115 words each.

Written for: the task reviewers.

```
Aesthetics: Website A
Website A is better looking because its timeline reads clean and complete. Main room bookings sit in solid dark green bars, and each appliance gets its own soft color, with peach for the oven, lilac for the hob, pink for the mixer, blue for the microwave and mint for the dishwasher, plus round initial badges and diagonal hatching wherever the room isn't reserved. Every sample bar shows the full name and time. Website B's warm cream and orange look is friendly, but its one-hour bars get cut off, like "Jamie Park 08:00 - 09:..." and "Alex Mor... 13:15 - 14:...". Website A's wide sidebar does squeeze its timeline to about six hours at a time.

Functionality: Website A
Website A is stronger on function because it follows every rule and always explains itself. Clicking an appliance slot outside a room booking shows "A little room first" with a Book the room button, an appliance booking that runs past the room is refused with a clear message, a clash with another booking is blocked, and cancelling a room warns that its appliance bookings go too. Website B handles the room-first rule, overlaps and the cancel warning just as well, but when a time runs past the room, pressing Confirm booking just closes the window with nothing saved and no explanation, and its short bars hide part of the user name and time range.

Overall: Website A
Website A is the better overall choice. Website B has some nice touches, like a sidebar that folds into icons so more hours fit on screen and "Book the room" hints right inside the main room row, and its booking rules hold up. Still, Website A feels more finished: its color-coded appliance bars show every user and time range in full, its hatched no-room areas and Book the room prompt make the room-first rule obvious, and every refused booking comes with a plain reason. Its only real drawback is the wide sidebar that limits the timeline to about six hours at a time, which matters less than Website B's cut-off names and silent Confirm button.
```

content.text:
For task 3991159, Aesthetics is a tie and Website A wins Functionality and Overall. Website A is "Stratify" (saved_resource.html) and Website B is "Stratlab" (saved_resource(1).html).

**What both sites do:**
- sort the leaderboard
- filter by market, timeframe, minimum win rate, maximum drawdown and number of trades
- open strategy details and side-by-side compare with all eight requested metrics
- run backtests with adjustable parameters
- switch between live and historical data
- list TradingView, Alpaca and Interactive Brokers
- pause and resume scanning

**The deciding difference:** when scanning is paused, Website A's trade feed badge changes from "Live" to "Paused" and the button becomes "Start scanning". Website B's header says Paused, but every leaderboard row keeps a green "Running" tag. That's the same kind of wrong-status flaw the reviewer used to flip 1210318.

**Weak spots named for each site:**
- **Website A:** its wide sidebar squeezes the tables, and its sample backtest shows an unlikely 16.67 Sharpe ratio.
- **Website B:** its trade prices and table text are small and gray.

**Checks:** all reasons pass, with one paragraph each, straight quotes, no stiff words, and 112–119 words.

Written for: the task reviewers.

```
Aesthetics: Both are good
Both Website A and Website B are good because each one looks like a clean, professional trading desk in white and green. Website A pairs a filled green equity curve and a dashed S&P 500 line with color-coded win rate pills, red drawdown numbers and a small 7D trend line on every leaderboard row. Website B tops its page with four stat cards that each carry a mini chart, then uses market badges, green Sharpe pills and status tags in its leaderboard, and its sidebar folds into icons to leave more room. Website A's sidebar stays wide and squeezes its tables, and Website B's trade prices and table text are small and gray, but neither issue changes the call.

Functionality: Website A
Website A is stronger on function because its scanner shows the real state at all times. Pressing Pause scanner switches the trade feed badge from Live to Paused, turns the button into Start scanning and stops new trades from coming in. Website B pauses too, but every strategy in its leaderboard keeps a green Running tag. Beyond that, the two match closely: both sort the leaderboard, filter by market, timeframe, minimum win rate, maximum drawdown and trade count, compare strategies side by side with profit factor and trade duration, run backtests, switch between live and historical data, and list TradingView, Alpaca and Interactive Brokers. Website A's sample backtest does show an unlikely 16.67 Sharpe ratio.

Overall: Website A
Website A is the better overall pick. Website B has real strengths, like stat cards with mini charts, a sidebar that folds away, and backtests that land in a saved history table, and its features cover nearly the whole request. Website A matches it feature for feature with its own clean green look, 7D trend lines on each strategy and a filter panel that can also narrow results by strategy type. What tips it is trust: when Website A's scanner is paused, its labels say Paused, while Website B keeps telling users that every strategy is still Running, which matters a lot for a tool meant to judge strategies before real money goes in.
```

content.text:
Website A wins all three for task 3992127, the drag-and-drop puzzle game. Website A is "pieceful" (saved_resource.html) and Website B is "puzzl." (saved_resource(1).html). I finished both puzzles with real mouse drags inside the 800px review frame.

- **Drag and drop:** works on both.
  - A correct drop snaps the piece in with "A perfect fit".
  - A wrong drop sends it back ("Not quite its spot" on Website A, "Not quite" on Website B).
  - Finishing shows a completion card.
- **Shared controls:** both have hints, shuffle, three difficulty levels and a picture preview.
- **The deciding difference:** Website B's puzzle photo (alpine-escape.jpg) never loads.
  - Its pieces show as blurry gray and blue blobs.
  - Broken-image icons and alt text appear in the puzzle thumbnail, the Preview window, the "Completed Alpine escape puzzle" finish card and all five puzzles in Browse puzzles.
  - Following the 3988061 feedback, I treated this as a Functionality failure as well as a visual one.
- **Website A's pictures all load:** the pastel seaside cottage painting, plus two photo scenes (a hot-air balloon and a rocky coast) that work as puzzles.
- **Weak spot named for Website A:** its pale sky and water pieces are hard to tell apart.

All reasons pass the checks: one paragraph each, straight quotes, no stiff words, 113–118 words.

Written for: the task reviewers.

```
Aesthetics: Website A
Website A is the clear choice for looks because its puzzle art actually shows up. The board holds a soft pastel painting of a seaside cottage with a red roof, cypress trees and a yellow sun, the tray pieces tilt at playful angles, and the scene picker offers photo thumbnails like a hot-air balloon and a rocky coast. Website B has a tidy layout with a bold green header, but its pictures never load, so the pieces are blurry gray and blue blobs and broken image icons sit in the puzzle thumbnail, the preview window and every card in the collection. Website A's pale sky and water pieces do look a lot alike.

Functionality: Website A
Website A works better as a puzzle game because every part of it shows what it should. Dragging a piece onto the right spot snaps it in with "A perfect fit," a wrong spot sends it back with "Not quite its spot," Hint names the exact row and column, Preview opens the full picture, and Easy, Medium and Hard switch between 12, 20 and 30 pieces. Website B's drag and drop works just as well, with the same kind of hint, shuffle and three difficulty levels, but its puzzle image fails to load, so the preview window, the finished card and all five puzzles in Browse puzzles show broken image icons instead of pictures.

Overall: Website A
Website A is preferred overall. Website B has a clean layout, a puzzle collection sorted into Nature, Coast and Botanical, and drag and drop that snaps pieces in just as smoothly, so the game itself holds up. The trouble is that a jigsaw lives on its picture, and Website B's photos never appear, leaving blurry placeholder pieces and broken image icons across the board, preview, finished card and collection. Website A gives players a finished painted scene, two more photo puzzles to pick from, a finish card with time, pieces and moves, and the same hint and difficulty options. Its soft pastel pieces can be hard to tell apart, but that's a small price next to missing pictures.
```

For task 3987199 (Rift & Ember restaurant site), Website A wins Aesthetics and Overall, and Functionality is a tie. Both websites are titled "Rift & Ember". Website A is saved_resource.html and Website B is saved_resource(1).html.

One thing about the saved files: most dish and scene photos are missing on both sites, because they load lazily and were never downloaded when the page was saved. Only the two hero images were saved. That hits both sites the same way, so I didn't count it against either. I filled the gaps with placeholders so I could judge the layouts, and kept photo contents out of the reasons.

- **Works on both:**
  - the Three.js ember particles running all the way down to the footer, and an ember-dot cursor
  - hero text that tilts with the mouse, a grain overlay and an animated hero plate
  - a kinetic facts scroller in Our Story, and menu cards with 3D tilt and amber glow
  - menu filters and dish detail windows, plus the horizontal Experience scenes with arrows
  - a booking form that blocks a blank name and shows a summary after submitting
- **Where Website A matches the brief more closely:**
  - Its glass panels cover the menu cards, dish labels and story caption. Website B only uses glass on the booking form.
  - Its hero has a real round plate floating in a turning text ring.
  - It adds a "View the full menu" window.
- **Weak spots named:**
  - Website A's hero text under the tagline is small, and its form asks for an email the brief didn't list.
  - Website B has no way to see more than its six dishes.

All reasons pass the checks: one paragraph each, straight quotes, no stiff words, 107–122 words.

Written for: the task reviewers.

```
Aesthetics: Website A
Website A has the stronger look, mostly because it follows the requested style more closely. Its hero sets a giant serif RIFT & EMBER beside a round plate of fire-roasted lamb that floats inside a slowly turning text ring, just like the animated plate the brief asked for. Further down, the menu cards are frosted glass panels with little tags like THE SIGNATURE and FIRE-KISSED, and the story photo carries a glassy Made of this place caption. Website B is cinematic too, with a centered title over a full-width seared steak, but its menu cards are solid dark panels and only the booking form gets the glass look. Website A's small hero text under the tagline is a bit hard to read.

Functionality: Both are good
Both Website A and Website B are good on function, since every requested piece works on each. Embers drift behind the page into the footer, an ember dot replaces the cursor, the hero title tilts with the mouse, menu cards tilt and glow when hovered, the menu filters sort dishes by type, each dish opens a detail window, the Experience arrows slide between the three scenes, and the booking form blocks a blank name and then shows a summary. Website A also adds a full menu window, though its form asks for an email the brief never listed, while Website B has no way to see more than its six signature dishes.

Overall: Website A
Website A is the better overall pick. Website B delivers the same working pieces, from the tilting cards to the booking summary, and its full-width steak hero is a strong first impression. Website A wins on how closely it matches the brief, with a floating plate in the hero, frosted glass menu cards with amber hover glow, a glassy caption on the story photo, and an extra full menu window for anyone who wants more than the six signatures. Its tiny hero text is a small miss, but Website B's lack of glass panels outside the booking form leaves it a step further from the requested look.
```
