content.content:
1	# UI Berry: Website Preference Tasks
2	
3	## 1. What I Provide
4	- A **Task ID**. The folder with that name holds the task HTML (instructions and the User request) and the saved files for Website A and Website B. Sometimes they come zipped.
5	- Screenshots of both websites (optional, and often cut off).
6	- Reviewer feedback from earlier tasks in `Prompt/Feedback.md`. Read it before every task.
7	
8	When a new Task ID comes in, work only from that folder. Never reuse content from a previous task.
9	
10	---
11	
12	## 2. Task Types
13	
14	### Type 1: Aesthetics / Functionality / Overall
15	Three independent picks. Each one is **A is better / B is better / Both are good / Both are bad**.
16	- **Aesthetics:** visual quality only (layout, composition, typography, color, polish, spacing, visual defects). Ignore whether controls work.
17	- **Functionality:** behavior and prompt-following only. Does the requested content render, and do the links, buttons, controls, navigation and interactions work? Ignore polish unless broken rendering blocks the check.
18	- **Overall:** the complete experience, weighing looks and function together. It doesn't have to match the other two picks.
19	
20	### Type 2: Editing A/B Preference (Before / After)
21	Two independent picks: **Satisfaction** and **Overall**.
22	- Each tab (Website A, Website B) shows a split screen with **Before Edit** on the left and **After Edit** on the right. Judge the **After Edit** side. The Before page is usually the same for both.
23	- **Satisfaction:** does the After site do what the edit request asked? Are the requested parts there, and do they work? Ignore polish unless it blocks use.
24	- **Overall:** the **whole After website**, not just the new feature. That means the hero section, images, navigation bar, every section, all buttons, the requested feature, and how it all looks and works together.
25	
26	### Which file is which
27	In the task HTML, the first iframe sits in the "Website A" tab and the second in the "Website B" tab. Usually Website A is `saved_resource.html` and Website B is `saved_resource(1).html`. For editing tasks, open each of those two wrapper files to find its Before and After files.
28	
29	A site that fails to load, freezes or can't be inspected counts as a **functionality failure**.
30	
31	---
32	
33	## 3. How to Evaluate
34	
35	### 3.1 Start with the request
36	Read the User request and turn it into a checklist of every concrete requirement:
37	- the elements and content asked for
38	- colors and style
39	- modes (for example T20 and ODI, batting and bowling)
40	- behaviors (hover, scroll, export)
41	- limits (for example "just one page, no extra views")
42	
43	Every requirement gets checked on both websites.
44	
45	### 3.2 Test the way the reviewer does
46	Reviewers use each site inside the task page: a frame about **1000px wide and 800px tall**. Editing panes are only about **480–680px wide**. Test there, with real mouse clicks, hovers and key presses.
47	- Click **every** button, tab, filter, toggle, card, tile and menu item, and note what each one does. Note the ones that do nothing. Footer and legal links only need one quick pass (see 3.6).
48	- Make sure menu items and buttons are clickable across their whole area, not just one spot.
49	- Hover **every** tooltip, bubble and hotspot.
50	- Open **every** gallery or collection item and look at each card up close for overlaps, cut-off text and broken labels.
51	- On forms, try blank input and bad input.
52	- On games and tools, run the core loop once in **each requested mode**.
53	- Take one full-size look for the overall visual impression.
54	
55	### 3.3 What counts as evidence
56	- **Only what a reviewer sees in normal use** within a minute or two of playing or clicking. If a state takes a long play-through (a final match result, a later stage), describe it through what's visible on the page instead: the scoreboard, the buttons, the rules text, the target shown.
57	- **Never use as evidence:**
58	  - whether a file download works (downloads are blocked in the review frame; a menu item that can't be clicked is still a valid point)
59	  - phone or mobile layout
60	  - timing or speed numbers
61	  - console messages
62	  - flaws that only show at one window size
63	  - **anything learned from the code or network traffic** rather than from the screen: which backend endpoints get called, FormData, how a game is programmed (1210318: the backend claims were removed)
64	  - **anything that depends on saved browser storage:** a best score or draft kept after a reload, "saved in this browser" (3978133: the reviewer's panel may block storage)
65	- **Broken or missing images count against a site.** If a picture fails to load (a broken-image icon, alt text, an empty dark box where a photo should be), the reviewer sees it too. Treat it as a Functionality failure (content doesn't render), and mention it in Aesthetics if it leaves a visible hole. Never wave it off as a problem with the saved files (3988061: Functionality was flipped to the side with all images showing).
66	- **Measure before comparing sizes.** Never call one element "tiny" or "bigger" from a scaled-down screenshot. Compare the actual pixel sizes first (3978133: Website B's bird was really the same size as Website A's).
67	- **A feature both sites have is never a difference.** Before crediting one site, confirm the other doesn't have it too, and call shared features shared.
68	- **Before calling something an advantage, look at it again.** If it could just as easily be read as a flaw, leave it out.
69	- **Don't over-claim.** Describe only what was actually shown on the page.
70	
71	### 3.4 What to check under each lens
72	
73	**Aesthetics**
74	- Match to the requested look: colors, style and shape (for example a pink, yellow and cyan banner, a soft rounded star, brand colors).
75	- The main visual (hero, logo, model, chart, character), with a specific detail of how it's drawn. Example: "a crate drawn as a flat dark green silhouette with only the carrot in color".
76	- Layout and spacing: crowded areas, alignment, balance, empty space. **Look for uneven columns and empty gaps**, such as a card that ends early and leaves a blank area under it while the column next to it keeps going (1210318: an empty dark gap under Website B's email preview card decided Aesthetics).
77	- The frame and page style: a dark cabinet or frame around the main area, the title treatment, the page background color (3978133: "the dark arcade cabinet and red title of Website A against the sage page of Website B").
78	- Typography and readability: text over photos, pale labels fading into the background, contrast.
79	- Visible defects: overlaps (for example "the seventh fish overlaps its text"), cut-off text, wrong labels, elements covering other content.
80	- Consistency and polish across sections, cards and icons.
81	
82	**Functionality**
83	- Each item on the request checklist: present, and does it work?
84	- Each control named with its result (for example "the Earnings chip filters the bubbles", "the ODI card switches to 50 overs").
85	- Dead or half-working controls named exactly (for example "code tiles do nothing on click", "the portfolio and settings buttons lead nowhere").
86	- Options counted (for example "three backgrounds and an SVG-only download", "five body colors").
87	- Working features only one site has (for example "only Website B opens each logo in a larger preview").
88	- Navigation: menu links, tabs and pages actually open.
89	- Forms: whether they reject blank or invalid input.
90	- Modes and state: requested modes switch and reset works. Don't credit anything that only shows after a reload (see 3.3).
91	- **Status labels that don't match the real state** count as functionality bugs, for example a card still showing "Live" while sending is paused, or a "Running" badge on a finished campaign (1210318). Never dismiss these as minor.
92	- Content that should show but doesn't: broken images, empty panels, missing pictures (3988061).
93	- Following the request's limits: extra pages or views the request said not to add.
94	- **Visual details never go in Functionality** (for example a pale banner or a crowded layout).
95	
96	**Satisfaction (editing tasks)**
97	- Each requested change is in the After site, works with a real click, and does the whole job. For example, it scrolls all the way to the bottom, and the go-to-top button at the bottom takes the page back to the top.
98	- Ignore polish unless it blocks use.
99	
100	**Overall**
101	- Cover the whole site: hero, images, navigation bar, sections, all buttons, and the requested features.
102	- Weigh at least one visual point against at least one behavior point.
103	- If both sites are strong and **no visible flaw separates them**, choose **Both are good**. If one site has a visible flaw the other doesn't (a broken image, an empty gap, a wrong status label, a dead button), pick the cleaner site, even when the flaw is small (1210318: three ties were flipped to Website A over small visible flaws). Choose **Both are bad** when both fail the core request.
104	- When Aesthetics and Functionality both go to the same site, Overall usually goes there too.
105	
106	### 3.5 Decision rules
107	- Each question is judged on its own. Overall can differ from the others.
108	- Decide by the **biggest, most visible difference in that lens**, not by counting small nitpicks.
109	- Ties are allowed, but only when the sites really are even **after checking for visible flaws on both**. Ties held on 3987088 and 3979081 and were overturned on 1210318.
110	- **Every site has a weak spot.** Before deciding, write down at least one visible weakness for each site.
111	- The option picked in the form must match what the reason says.
112	
113	### 3.6 Steps to skip or keep short
114	These have never changed a verdict or a reason, so don't spend time on them.
115	
116	**Skip:**

# UI Berry: Website Preference Tasks

## 1. What I Provide
- A **Task ID**. The folder with that name holds the task HTML (instructions and the User request) and the saved files for Website A and Website B. Sometimes they come zipped.
- Screenshots of both websites (optional, and often cut off).
- Reviewer feedback from earlier tasks in `Prompt/Feedback.md`. Read it before every task.

When a new Task ID comes in, work only from that folder. Never reuse content from a previous task.

---

## 2. Task Types

### Type 1: Aesthetics / Functionality / Overall
Three independent picks. Each one is **A is better / B is better / Both are good / Both are bad**.
- **Aesthetics:** visual quality only (layout, composition, typography, color, polish, spacing, visual defects). Ignore whether controls work.
- **Functionality:** behavior and prompt-following only. Does the requested content render, and do the links, buttons, controls, navigation and interactions work? Ignore polish unless broken rendering blocks the check.
- **Overall:** the complete experience, weighing looks and function together. It doesn't have to match the other two picks.

### Type 2: Editing A/B Preference (Before / After)
Two independent picks: **Satisfaction** and **Overall**.
- Each tab (Website A, Website B) shows a split screen with **Before Edit** on the left and **After Edit** on the right. Judge the **After Edit** side. The Before page is usually the same for both.
- **Satisfaction:** does the After site do what the edit request asked? Are the requested parts there, and do they work? Ignore polish unless it blocks use.
- **Overall:** the **whole After website**, not just the new feature. That means the hero section, images, navigation bar, every section, all buttons, the requested feature, and how it all looks and works together.

### Which file is which
In the task HTML, the first iframe sits in the "Website A" tab and the second in the "Website B" tab. Usually Website A is `saved_resource.html` and Website B is `saved_resource(1).html`. For editing tasks, open each of those two wrapper files to find its Before and After files.

A site that fails to load, freezes or can't be inspected counts as a **functionality failure**.

---

## 3. How to Evaluate

### 3.1 Start with the request
Read the User request and turn it into a checklist of every concrete requirement:
- the elements and content asked for
- colors and style
- modes (for example T20 and ODI, batting and bowling)
- behaviors (hover, scroll, export)
- limits (for example "just one page, no extra views")

Every requirement gets checked on both websites.

### 3.2 Test the way the reviewer does
Reviewers use each site inside the task page: a frame about **1000px wide and 800px tall**. Editing panes are only about **480–680px wide**. Test there, with real mouse clicks, hovers and key presses.
- Click **every** button, tab, filter, toggle, card, tile and menu item, and note what each one does. Note the ones that do nothing. Footer and legal links only need one quick pass (see 3.6).
- Make sure menu items and buttons are clickable across their whole area, not just one spot.
- Hover **every** tooltip, bubble and hotspot.
- Open **every** gallery or collection item and look at each card up close for overlaps, cut-off text and broken labels.
- On forms, try blank input and bad input.
- On games and tools, run the core loop once in **each requested mode**.
- Take one full-size look for the overall visual impression.

### 3.3 What counts as evidence
- **Only what a reviewer sees in normal use** within a minute or two of playing or clicking. If a state takes a long play-through (a final match result, a later stage), describe it through what's visible on the page instead: the scoreboard, the buttons, the rules text, the target shown.
- **Never use as evidence:**
  - whether a file download works (downloads are blocked in the review frame; a menu item that can't be clicked is still a valid point)
  - phone or mobile layout
  - timing or speed numbers
  - console messages
  - flaws that only show at one window size
  - **anything learned from the code or network traffic** rather than from the screen: which backend endpoints get called, FormData, how a game is programmed (1210318: the backend claims were removed)
  - **anything that depends on saved browser storage:** a best score or draft kept after a reload, "saved in this browser" (3978133: the reviewer's panel may block storage)
- **Broken or missing images count against a site.** If a picture fails to load (a broken-image icon, alt text, an empty dark box where a photo should be), the reviewer sees it too. Treat it as a Functionality failure (content doesn't render), and mention it in Aesthetics if it leaves a visible hole. Never wave it off as a problem with the saved files (3988061: Functionality was flipped to the side with all images showing).
- **Measure before comparing sizes.** Never call one element "tiny" or "bigger" from a scaled-down screenshot. Compare the actual pixel sizes first (3978133: Website B's bird was really the same size as Website A's).
- **A feature both sites have is never a difference.** Before crediting one site, confirm the other doesn't have it too, and call shared features shared.
- **Before calling something an advantage, look at it again.** If it could just as easily be read as a flaw, leave it out.
- **Don't over-claim.** Describe only what was actually shown on the page.

### 3.4 What to check under each lens

**Aesthetics**
- Match to the requested look: colors, style and shape (for example a pink, yellow and cyan banner, a soft rounded star, brand colors).
- The main visual (hero, logo, model, chart, character), with a specific detail of how it's drawn. Example: "a crate drawn as a flat dark green silhouette with only the carrot in color".
- Layout and spacing: crowded areas, alignment, balance, empty space. **Look for uneven columns and empty gaps**, such as a card that ends early and leaves a blank area under it while the column next to it keeps going (1210318: an empty dark gap under Website B's email preview card decided Aesthetics).
- The frame and page style: a dark cabinet or frame around the main area, the title treatment, the page background color (3978133: "the dark arcade cabinet and red title of Website A against the sage page of Website B").
- Typography and readability: text over photos, pale labels fading into the background, contrast.
- Visible defects: overlaps (for example "the seventh fish overlaps its text"), cut-off text, wrong labels, elements covering other content.
- Consistency and polish across sections, cards and icons.

**Functionality**
- Each item on the request checklist: present, and does it work?
- Each control named with its result (for example "the Earnings chip filters the bubbles", "the ODI card switches to 50 overs").
- Dead or half-working controls named exactly (for example "code tiles do nothing on click", "the portfolio and settings buttons lead nowhere").
- Options counted (for example "three backgrounds and an SVG-only download", "five body colors").
- Working features only one site has (for example "only Website B opens each logo in a larger preview").
- Navigation: menu links, tabs and pages actually open.
- Forms: whether they reject blank or invalid input.
- Modes and state: requested modes switch and reset works. Don't credit anything that only shows after a reload (see 3.3).
- **Status labels that don't match the real state** count as functionality bugs, for example a card still showing "Live" while sending is paused, or a "Running" badge on a finished campaign (1210318). Never dismiss these as minor.
- Content that should show but doesn't: broken images, empty panels, missing pictures (3988061).
- Following the request's limits: extra pages or views the request said not to add.
- **Visual details never go in Functionality** (for example a pale banner or a crowded layout).

**Satisfaction (editing tasks)**
- Each requested change is in the After site, works with a real click, and does the whole job. For example, it scrolls all the way to the bottom, and the go-to-top button at the bottom takes the page back to the top.
- Ignore polish unless it blocks use.

**Overall**
- Cover the whole site: hero, images, navigation bar, sections, all buttons, and the requested features.
- Weigh at least one visual point against at least one behavior point.
- If both sites are strong and **no visible flaw separates them**, choose **Both are good**. If one site has a visible flaw the other doesn't (a broken image, an empty gap, a wrong status label, a dead button), pick the cleaner site, even when the flaw is small (1210318: three ties were flipped to Website A over small visible flaws). Choose **Both are bad** when both fail the core request.

- Each question is judged on its own. Overall can differ from the others.
- Decide by the **biggest, most visible difference in that lens**, not by counting small nitpicks.

- **Every site has a weak spot.** Before deciding, write down at least one visible weakness for each site.
- The option picked in the form must match what the reason says.

- **Automatic overlap scanners.** They flag decorative shapes and miss real overlaps. Look at close-up screenshots instead.
- **Hunting for flaws at many window sizes.** A flaw that shows at only one width can't be used.

**Keep short:**

- **Footer, legal and "About" links:** one quick pass to catch dead links. No need to read every dialog.
- **Reading the site's code:** only when it saves time. For example, decoding and comparing the Before/After source on editing tasks shows exactly what changed. Don't study game or 3D logic in depth.

  - Timing or speed numbers.
  - Console messages.
  - Flaws that only show at one window size.
  - **Anything learned from the code or network traffic**, such as endpoints called, FormData, or how a game is programmed (1210318).

- Layout and spacing: crowded areas, alignment, balance. Look for **uneven columns and empty gaps**, like a card that ends early and leaves a blank area while the next column keeps going (1210318).
- Typography and readability: text over photos, pale labels fading out, contrast.
- Visible defects: overlaps, cut-off text, wrong labels, elements covering content, broken images.
- Consistency and polish across sections, cards and icons.

- Working features only one site has, taken from the inventory in 3.3.
- Navigation: menu links, tabs and pages actually open.
- Forms: blank and invalid input are rejected or explained.

- Ignore polish unless it blocks use.

**Skip:**

- Phone or mobile screenshots.
- Measuring timing or speed.
- Reading console warnings.
- Automatic overlap scanners. Look at close-up screenshots instead.
- Hunting for flaws at many window sizes.

**Keep short:**
- One full-size look for the overall impression. The review-frame check is the one that counts.
- One quick pass over footer, legal and "About" links.

### 4.1 Hard rules (each one has cost points)

- **Name both sites in every reason.**
- **The first sentence is the verdict.**
- **Never address or name the reader.** No "you", "your", "users", "user", "visitors" or "people". Describe what the site does instead. Write "the leaderboard keeps every row tagged Running", not "it tells users every strategy is running" (3991159).

- **Straight apostrophes and quotes only** (`'` `"`). Never curly ones (`’` `“`). This was flagged on 3987088, 3979081, 3988061 and 3991159.
- **One paragraph per reason**, with no line breaks (3979081).
- **Third person only.** No "I", "me", "my" or "we".
- **No stiff connecting words** like "therefore", "thus", "hence", "moreover", "furthermore" or "additionally". Use "so", "but" and "and", or start a new sentence.
- No em dashes, and no filler like "seamless", "elevate" or "robust".
- **Never write "neither has a weak spot"**, "neither has a flaw" or "nothing is broken" (3979081).
- **No contradictions.** Don't call a site complete or equal while listing things it lacks (3991159).
- Only facts confirmed on screen (see 3.4). Don't mention how the sites were checked.

### 4.2 Allowed openings
The verdict comes first, with no category words:
- Website A is better because...
- Website A is the best option because...
- Website A is preferred because...
- Website A is stronger because...
- Ties: **Both Website A and Website B are good because...** or **Both Website A and Website B are bad because...**

Rotate the openings from task to task. The rest of each sentence should also vary in rhythm.

### 4.3 Templates
Each reason is one paragraph of 4–6 sentences and **80–110 words**. Use concrete on-screen words: colors, shapes, section names, button labels, exact messages.

**Aesthetics: Website X**
1. **Verdict and the main reason:** "Website X is better because its [main visual] [does what]."
2. **The winner's look, with three or more concrete details:** the main visual and how it's drawn, colors, layout or frame, title treatment.
3. **Another strength of the winner,** for example a section style, card design or readability.
4. **The other site's specific visible problem:** a broken image, empty gap, overlap, unreadable text, or a clear mismatch with the requested style. Name where it is.
5. **One honest weak spot of the winner,** kept small.

*Tie version:* "Both Website A and Website B are good because..."
- Describe each site's style with two or three concrete details.
- Name one specific weak spot for each site.
- End with why those don't change the call.

**Functionality: Website X**
1. **Verdict and the deciding behavior:** "Website X is stronger because [the control or behavior that decides it]."
2. **The winner's controls and their results:** three to five, each named with what it does.
3. **Shared features stated as shared:** "Both sort the leaderboard, filter by..., and...".
4. **The other site's exact gap:** a missing control named exactly, or a broken one with what happens. For example: "Website B's period buttons only change the dates on the chart."
5. **One honest weak spot of the winner,** if there is one.

*Tie version:*
- List the shared working features.
- Give each site's extra and one weak spot for each.
- Never include visual words.

**Overall: Website X** (write it last)
1. **Verdict:** "Website X is the best option because [deciding factor]."
2. **Fair credit to the other site,** with its real strengths named. Call its unique features unique.
3. **The winner's visual point:** one concrete detail.
4. **The winner's behavior point:** one control and its result.
5. **Why the deciding factor outweighs the other site's strengths,** with the winner's own small weak spot kept in proportion.

Overall must not repeat the Functionality sentences or say "matches everything".

### 4.4 Example (3991159, rewritten to the rules)
Functionality: Website A

> Website A is stronger because its controls change what they say they change. The period buttons redraw the equity line and its value axis for each range, Pause scanner switches the trade feed badge to Paused, and the filter panel can also narrow strategies by type. Both sites sort the leaderboard, filter by market, timeframe, win rate, drawdown and trade count, compare two strategies side by side and run backtests. Website B's period buttons only change the dates under its chart, and every strategy row keeps a green Running tag after scanning is paused.

---

## 5. Answer Format
Write the whole result in **one code block**.

Aesthetics / Functionality / Overall tasks:
```
Aesthetics: Website B
Reason paragraph

Functionality: Website A
Reason paragraph

Overall: Website A
Reason paragraph
```

Editing tasks:
```
Satisfaction: Both are good
Reason paragraph

Overall: Website B
Reason paragraph
```

**Before submitting:** paste the reasons exactly as written. Re-typing, translating, or running the text through grammar or rewrite tools can change "Website A" to "Web Site A", turn straight quotes curly, or add "you" and "users". All of these have cost points. If the text gets edited, re-run the checklist below.

---

## 6. Final Checklist (before submitting)
- [ ] Every requirement in the User request was checked on both websites.
- [ ] A control inventory was made (3.3), and each control's real effect was checked, not just its label (3.2).
- [ ] Each reason opens with the verdict, using an allowed opening (4.2).
- [ ] "Website A" and "Website B" are spelled exactly that way, and both appear in every reason.
- [ ] No "you", "your", "users", "user", "visitors" or "people". No category names (aesthetics, functionality, function, overall, satisfaction).
- [ ] Third person, no stiff connectors, no em dashes, only straight apostrophes and quotes, one paragraph per reason.
- [ ] Aesthetics has only visual points, and Functionality has only behavior points.
- [ ] Shared features are called shared, and unique features are called unique. No "matches everything" claims.
- [ ] Every failure claim was double-checked for an on-screen warning or explanation.
- [ ] No claims from code, network, storage, downloads, phone layouts or timing. Lazy-loading gaps shared by both sites are left out.
- [ ] Each page was checked for broken images, empty gaps, uneven columns and status labels that don't match the state.
- [ ] Ties are used only when nothing real separates the sites, and each tie names one weak spot per site.
- [ ] Each reason is 80–110 words (never under 40), counted.
- [ ] The opening style differs from the previous task.
- [ ] The pick in the form matches the reason.

---

## 7. Lessons from Reviewer Feedback
| Task | What went wrong | Rule now |
|---|---|---|
| 6250482 | "Less personality" with no evidence; "more limited" with no list | Describe exactly what's on screen; list exact options and dead controls |
| 6257531 | "Website is the better choice" with no letter | Name Website A and Website B in full in every reason |
| 6261407 | Talked about general layout and missed the real differences | Look for unique working features and visible overlaps on every item |
| 6264396 | First person; a phone claim that couldn't be confirmed | Third person only; no phone claims; name each control and its result |
| 6255409 | First person; verdict not stated first | Open with the verdict sentence |
| 6250470 | Said downloads worked when menu items weren't fully clickable; "fewer controls" | Never claim downloads; check click areas; name exactly what's missing |
| 6251496 / 6243305 | Overall copied Functionality; a reason had only 35 words | Write Overall last with one point from each lens; count words |
| 6241898 | Credited one site with camera views both had; a visual point in Functionality; a flaw called an advantage | Check each control is really unique; keep the lenses separate; double-check every advantage |
| 6265185 | Typos and thin details | Proofread; add specific supporting details |
| 6253775 | Described end-of-match states the reviewer never reached | Use only what's visible in normal use |
| 6260728 | Tie reason didn't open with the tie; wrong form pick; Overall only covered the new buttons | Open with the tie sentence; check the form pick; Overall covers the whole site |
| 3987088 (4) | Ties right; but curly apostrophes, "A's" alone, "therefore" | Straight apostrophes; "Website A" in full; no formal connectors |
| 3979081 (4) | "Neither site has a weak spot"; a line break in a reason; curly apostrophes | Name a weak spot for each site; one paragraph; straight apostrophes |
| 3988061 (4) | Functionality tied although Website A showed broken firearm images; unclear openings | Broken images are a functionality failure; clear verdict openings |
| 1210318 (3) | Missed an empty gap and a "Live" label shown while paused; backend claims came from code | Check gaps and status labels; on-screen evidence only; real defects break ties |
| 3977933 (3) | Aesthetics and Overall too general and brief | 80–110 words with concrete details in every reason |
| 3978133 (4) | Called a same-size bird "tiny"; credited a best score kept after reload | Measure sizes; no storage or reload claims |
| 3979206 (4) | Called cut-off names in one-hour bars a flaw (should be a tie); said Website B gave no explanation when its form showed a warning; missed Website A's extra "All resources" filter | Normal compact UI isn't a flaw; on-screen warnings count as explanations; inventory every control, since one extra filter can decide Functionality |
| 3991159 (2) | Submitted text had "Web Site A/B" and curly apostrophes; missed that Website B's chart period buttons only change the dates; Overall said Website A covered everything while naming Website B-only features; used "you", "users" and category names | Exact "Website A/B"; verify each control's real effect; no "matches everything" claims; never "you", "users" or category words; paste text exactly |

# UI Berry: Website Preference Tasks

## 1. What I Provide
- A **Task ID**. The folder with that name holds the task HTML (instructions and the User request) and the saved files for Website A and Website B. Sometimes they come zipped.
- Screenshots of both websites (optional, and often cut off).
- Reviewer feedback from earlier tasks in `Prompt/Feedback.md`. Read it before every task.

When a new Task ID comes in, work only from that folder. Never reuse content from a previous task.

**Per-task workflow:**
1. Evaluate (section 3).
2. Write the three reasons with the templates (section 4).
3. Run the final checklist (section 6).
4. Give the answer in one code block, and append it to the end of `Feedback.md` with an empty `## Feedback:` slot.
5. When feedback arrives, add a row to section 7 and update the rules.

---

## 2. Task Types

### Type 1: Aesthetics / Functionality / Overall
Three independent picks. Each one is **A is better / B is better / Both are good / Both are bad**.
- **Aesthetics:** visual quality only: layout, composition, typography, color, polish, spacing and visual defects. Ignore whether controls work.
- **Functionality:** behavior and prompt-following only. Does the requested content render, and do the links, buttons, controls, navigation and interactions work? Ignore polish unless broken rendering blocks the check.
- **Overall:** the complete experience, weighing looks and behavior together. It doesn't have to match the other two picks.

### Type 2: Editing A/B Preference (Before / After)
Two independent picks: **Satisfaction** and **Overall**.
- Each tab (Website A, Website B) shows a split screen with **Before Edit** on the left and **After Edit** on the right. Judge the **After Edit** side. The Before page is usually the same for both.
- **Satisfaction:** does the After site do what the edit request asked? Are the requested parts there, and do they work? Ignore polish unless it blocks use.
- **Overall:** the **whole After website**, not just the new feature. That covers the hero section, images, navigation bar, every section, all buttons and the requested feature, and how they look and work together.

### Which file is which
In the task HTML, the first iframe sits in the "Website A" tab and the second in the "Website B" tab. Usually Website A is `saved_resource.html` and Website B is `saved_resource(1).html`. For editing tasks, open each wrapper file to find its Before and After files.

A site that fails to load, freezes or can't be inspected counts as a **functionality failure**.

---

## 3. How to Evaluate

### 3.1 Start with the request
Turn the User request into a checklist of every concrete requirement:
- elements and content
- colors and style
- modes
- behaviors
- limits, for example "just one page"

Check every item on both websites.

### 3.2 Test the way the reviewer does
Reviewers use each site inside the task page: a frame about **1000px wide and 800px tall**. Editing panes are only about **480–680px wide**. Test there, with real mouse clicks, hovers, drags and key presses.
- Click **every** button, tab, filter, toggle, card, tile and menu item, and note what each one does. Note the ones that do nothing. Footer and legal links only need one quick pass (see 3.6).
- **Check that each control changes the thing it claims to change, not just a label.** Compare the affected element before and after:
  - A chart's range buttons must redraw the line and the value axis, not only swap the date labels (3991159: Website B's period buttons only changed the dates).
  - A filter must change the list.
  - A Pause button must stop the updates and change every status label.
- Make sure menu items and buttons can be clicked across their whole area.
- Hover **every** tooltip, bubble and hotspot.
- Open **every** gallery or collection item and look at each card up close for overlaps, cut-off text and broken labels.
- On forms, try blank input and bad input. Note any warning text shown inside the form; that counts as an explanation (3979206).
- On games and tools, run the core loop once in **each requested mode**.
- Take one full-size look for the overall visual impression.

### 3.3 Build a control inventory (mandatory)
Before deciding anything, write a side-by-side list of **every control and feature on each site**, and mark each one:
- **Shared**: both have it and it works on both.
- **Only on Website A** or **only on Website B**: name it exactly, for example "an All resources filter on the schedule".
- **Broken or half-working**: say exactly what fails, for example "the period buttons only change the dates".

The inventory decides Functionality and keeps Overall honest. One extra working control can be the whole reason one site wins:
- 3979206: Website A's extra "All resources" filter decided Functionality.
- 3991159: Overall was marked down for saying Website A covered everything while naming features only Website B had.

### 3.4 What counts as evidence
- **Only what a reviewer sees on screen in normal use**, within a minute or two of clicking or playing. Describe longer flows through what's visible: scoreboards, buttons, rules text, targets.
- **Never use as evidence:**
  - Whether a file download works. Downloads are blocked in the review frame. A menu item that can't be clicked is still a valid point.
  - Phone or mobile layout.
  - Timing or speed numbers.
  - Console messages.
  - Flaws that only show at one window size.
  - **Anything learned from the code or network traffic**, such as endpoints called, FormData, or how a game is programmed (1210318).

The field label already says it (3991159). Write "Website A is the best option because...", not "Website A is the better overall pick".
+- **Straight apostrophes and quotes only** (`'` `"`). Never curly ones (`’` `“`). This was flagged on 3987088, 3979081, 3988061 and 3991159.

```
Aesthetics: Both are good
Both Website A and Website B are good because each one turns a heavy subject into a calm, polished page. Website A pairs a cream background with an illustrated heart, a serif Pulse of America title with America in terracotta, and a state map shaded from pale tan to deep rust. Website B goes bolder, with a glossy red 3D heart that gently moves on its own, a burgundy band of 100 small figures with 20 of them lit up, and red bars for each age group. Website A's two-letter state labels are tiny, and Website B's source notes and bar labels are small and pale, but neither issue changes the call.

Functionality: Website A
Website A is stronger because it shows exactly where heart disease hits Americans hardest and lets every number be explored. Hovering a state shows its percentage, clicking it opens that state's story, the Mortality tab redraws the map in deaths per 100,000, the All adults, Women and Men menu recolors the map and updates the top five, and the List view sorts all 50 states. Both sites show a 1 in 5 deaths chart, open a sources window and end with a personal next-steps tool. Website B breaks high blood pressure down by age and sex, but its Coronary artery disease tab shows only one bar for all adults. Website A's state figures are marked as illustrative.

Overall: Website A
Website A is the best option because it answers the question of which Americans suffer most from heart disease. Website B makes a striking first impression with its glossy 3D heart and burgundy band of figures, and its high blood pressure numbers by age and sex come from the CDC. Website A counters with a warm, tidy layout and a shaded state map that works from end to end, with hover percentages, state stories, a Mortality tab and a Women and Men filter, plus a three-step heart check that ends with next steps. Its state numbers are only illustrative, but Website B never breaks heart disease itself down by group.
