1	# UI Berry: Website Preference Tasks
2	
3	## 1. What I Provide
4	- A **Task ID**. The folder with that name holds the task HTML (instructions and the User request) and the saved files for Website A and Website B. Sometimes they come zipped.
5	- Screenshots of both websites (optional, and often cut off).
6	- Reviewer feedback from earlier tasks in `Prompt/Feedback.md`. Read it before every task.
7	
8	When a new Task ID comes in, work only from that folder. Never reuse content from a previous task.
9	
10	**Per-task workflow:**
11	1. Evaluate (section 3).
12	2. Write the three reasons with the templates (section 4).
13	3. Run the final checklist (section 6).
14	4. Give the answer in one code block, and append it to the end of `Feedback.md` with an empty `## Feedback:` slot.
15	5. When feedback arrives, add a row to section 7 and update the rules.
16	
17	---
18	
19	## 2. Task Types
20	
21	### Type 1: Aesthetics / Functionality / Overall
22	Three independent picks. Each one is **A is better / B is better / Both are good / Both are bad**.
23	- **Aesthetics:** visual quality only: layout, composition, typography, color, polish, spacing and visual defects. Ignore whether controls work.
24	- **Functionality:** behavior and prompt-following only. Does the requested content render, and do the links, buttons, controls, navigation and interactions work? Ignore polish unless broken rendering blocks the check.
25	- **Overall:** the complete experience, weighing looks and behavior together. It doesn't have to match the other two picks.
26	
27	### Type 2: Editing A/B Preference (Before / After)
28	Two independent picks: **Satisfaction** and **Overall**.
29	- Each tab (Website A, Website B) shows a split screen with **Before Edit** on the left and **After Edit** on the right. Judge the **After Edit** side. The Before page is usually the same for both.
30	- **Satisfaction:** does the After site do what the edit request asked? Are the requested parts there, and do they work? Ignore polish unless it blocks use.
31	- **Overall:** the **whole After website**, not just the new feature. That covers the hero section, images, navigation bar, every section, all buttons and the requested feature, and how they look and work together.
32	
33	### Which file is which
34	In the task HTML, the first iframe sits in the "Website A" tab and the second in the "Website B" tab. Usually Website A is `saved_resource.html` and Website B is `saved_resource(1).html`. For editing tasks, open each wrapper file to find its Before and After files.
35	
36	A site that fails to load, freezes or can't be inspected counts as a **functionality failure**.
37	
38	---
39	
40	## 3. How to Evaluate
41	
42	### 3.1 Start with the request
43	Turn the User request into a checklist of every concrete requirement:
44	- elements and content
45	- colors and style
46	- modes
47	- behaviors
48	- limits, for example "just one page"
49	
50	Check every item on both websites.
51	
52	### 3.2 Test the way the reviewer does
53	Reviewers use each site inside the task page: a frame about **1000px wide and 800px tall**. Editing panes are only about **480–680px wide**. Test there, with real mouse clicks, hovers, drags and key presses.
54	- Click **every** button, tab, filter, toggle, card, tile and menu item, and note what each one does. Note the ones that do nothing. Footer and legal links only need one quick pass (see 3.6).
55	- **Check that each control changes the thing it claims to change, not just a label.** Compare the affected element before and after:
56	  - A chart's range buttons must redraw the line and the value axis, not only swap the date labels (3991159: Website B's period buttons only changed the dates).
57	  - A filter must change the list.
58	  - A Pause button must stop the updates and change every status label.
59	- Make sure menu items and buttons can be clicked across their whole area.
60	- Hover **every** tooltip, bubble and hotspot.
61	- Open **every** gallery or collection item and look at each card up close for overlaps, cut-off text and broken labels.
62	- On forms, try blank input and bad input. Note any warning text shown inside the form; that counts as an explanation (3979206).
63	- On games and tools, run the core loop once in **each requested mode**.
64	- Take one full-size look for the overall visual impression.
65	
66	### 3.3 Build a control inventory (mandatory)
67	Before deciding anything, write a side-by-side list of **every control and feature on each site**, and mark each one:
68	- **Shared**: both have it and it works on both.
69	- **Only on Website A** or **only on Website B**: name it exactly, for example "an All resources filter on the schedule".
70	- **Broken or half-working**: say exactly what fails, for example "the period buttons only change the dates".
71	
72	The inventory decides Functionality and keeps Overall honest. One extra working control can be the whole reason one site wins:
73	- 3979206: Website A's extra "All resources" filter decided Functionality.
74	- 3991159: Overall was marked down for saying Website A covered everything while naming features only Website B had.
75	
76	### 3.4 What counts as evidence
77	- **Only what a reviewer sees on screen in normal use**, within a minute or two of clicking or playing. Describe longer flows through what's visible: scoreboards, buttons, rules text, targets.
78	- **Never use as evidence:**
79	  - Whether a file download works. Downloads are blocked in the review frame. A menu item that can't be clicked is still a valid point.
80	  - Phone or mobile layout.
81	  - Timing or speed numbers.
82	  - Console messages.
83	  - Flaws that only show at one window size.
84	  - **Anything learned from the code or network traffic**, such as endpoints called, FormData, or how a game is programmed (1210318).
85	  - **Anything that depends on saved browser storage**, such as a best score or draft kept after a reload (3978133).
86	- **Broken or missing images:**
87	  - If a picture the page loads right away is missing, the reviewer sees it broken too. This means a broken-image icon, alt text, or an empty box where a photo should be.
88	  - That counts as a Functionality failure, and as an Aesthetics flaw when it leaves a visible hole (3988061).
89	  - Images marked `loading="lazy"` that are missing on **both** sites are a saving gap, not a site flaw. Judge the layout around them and leave them out of the reasons.
90	- **Normal production patterns are not flaws.** Text clipped inside a short timeline bar, ellipses in tight table cells and similar compact UI are normal (3979206: cut-off names in one-hour bars weren't accepted as a flaw).
91	- **Measure before comparing sizes.** Never call an element "tiny" or "bigger" from a scaled-down screenshot (3978133).
92	- **A feature both sites have is never a difference.** Before crediting one site, confirm the other doesn't have it too.
93	- **Look again before calling something an advantage.** If it could be read as a flaw, leave it out.
94	- **Look again before calling something a failure.** If the site showed a warning or reason anywhere on screen, it explained itself (3979206).
95	- **Only quote text that is visibly on screen.** Screen-reader-only text (hidden live regions, `sr-only` labels, `aria-label`s) doesn't count. Before quoting a message, confirm it appears in a screenshot (3992127: "Hint names the exact row and column" came from hidden text; on screen the hint only highlights the piece and its space).
96	- **Describe visuals exactly as a screenshot shows them.** Check colors, positions and which element moves before writing about them. Never infer relationships, such as "a plate inside a turning ring", when the badge actually sits at the plate's corner (3987199). Never call a white header with a green button a "bold green header" (3992127).
97	- **Zoom into every photo and illustration at full size** to look for artifacts: rainbow or color-banding patches, smeared AI details, distorted text, stretched images. These are the clearest visual flaws (3987199: rainbow patches in Website B's photos were missed).
98	- **Don't over-claim.** Describe only what was actually shown.
99	
100	### 3.5 What to check under each lens
101	
102	**Aesthetics**
103	- Match to the requested look: colors, style and shape.
104	- The main visual (hero, logo, model, chart, character), with a specific detail of how it's drawn. For example: "a crate drawn as a flat dark green silhouette with only the carrot in color".
105	- The frame and page style: a dark cabinet or frame, the title treatment, the page background color (3978133).
106	- Layout and spacing: crowded areas, alignment, balance. Look for **uneven columns and empty gaps**, like a card that ends early and leaves a blank area while the next column keeps going (1210318).
107	- Typography and readability: text over photos, pale labels fading out, contrast.
108	- Visible defects: overlaps, cut-off text, wrong labels, elements covering content, broken images.
109	- Consistency and polish across sections, cards and icons.
110	
111	**Functionality**
112	- Each item on the request checklist: is it present, and does it work?
113	- Each control named with its real result, checked as in 3.2.
114	- Dead or half-working controls named exactly: "code tiles do nothing on click", "the period buttons only change the dates".
115	- Options counted: "three backgrounds and an SVG-only download".
116	- Working features only one site has, taken from the inventory in 3.3.
117	- Navigation: menu links, tabs and pages actually open.
118	- Forms: blank and invalid input are rejected or explained.
119	- **Status labels that don't match the real state** are bugs, for example a "Live" or "Running" label shown while paused (1210318).
120	- Content that should show but doesn't: broken images, empty panels.
121	- **Visual details never go in Functionality.**
122	
123	**Satisfaction (editing tasks)**
124	- Each requested change is in the After site, works with a real click and does the whole job.
125	- Ignore polish unless it blocks use.
126	
127	**Overall**
128	- Cover the whole site: hero, images, navigation bar, sections, all buttons and the requested features.
129	- Weigh at least one visual point against at least one behavior point.
130	- Credit the other site's unique strengths **as unique**. Never write "matches it feature for feature", "covers everything the other has" or "does everything Website B does" unless the inventory shows that's literally true (3991159).
131	
132	### 3.6 Decision rules
133	- Each question is judged on its own. Overall can differ from the others.
134	- Decide by the **biggest real difference in that lens**, not by counting nitpicks.
135	- **Functionality:** a working extra control on one site, or a broken or half-working control on the other, decides it (3979206, 3991159, 1210318).
136	- **Aesthetics:** a real visible defect decides it: a broken image, an empty gap, an overlap or unreadable text. Different styles, or normal production compactness, are a tie: **Both are good** (3979206).
137	- **Ties** only when the inventory shows no real difference and neither site has a real visible defect. Ties held on 3987088, 3979081 and 3979206 (Aesthetics). They were overturned on 1210318, where a real defect existed.
138	- **Every site has a weak spot.** Write one down for each site before deciding.
139	- When Aesthetics and Functionality both go to the same site, Overall usually goes there too.
140	- The option picked in the form must match the reason.
141	
142	### 3.7 Steps to skip or keep short
143	**Skip:**
144	- Testing file downloads. Only check that the button or menu item can be clicked.
145	- Phone or mobile screenshots.
146	- Measuring timing or speed.
147	- Reading console warnings.
148	- Automatic overlap scanners. Look at close-up screenshots instead.
149	- Hunting for flaws at many window sizes.
150	
151	**Keep short:**
152	- One full-size look for the overall impression. The review-frame check is the one that counts.
153	- One quick pass over footer, legal and "About" links.
154	- Read the site's code only when it saves time. For example, compare Before/After source on editing tasks, or check `loading="lazy"` on missing images.
155	- Play each game mode's core loop once. No need to play to the end.
156	
157	---
158	
159	## 4. How to Write the Three Reasons
160	
161	### 4.1 Hard rules (each one has cost points)
162	- **Name the sites exactly "Website A" and "Website B"** every time. Never "Web Site A", "website a", "A", "B", "A's", "Site A", "Candidate 1" or "Website 1" (3991159, 3987088).
163	- **Name both sites in every reason.**
164	- **The first sentence is the verdict.**
165	- **Never address or name the reader.** No "you", "your", "users", "user", "visitors" or "people". Describe what the site does instead. Write "the leaderboard keeps every row tagged Running", not "it tells users every strategy is running" (3991159).
166	- **No category names inside a reason.** Don't write "aesthetics", "aesthetic", "functionality", "functional", "function", "overall" or "satisfaction" in the text. The field label already says it (3991159). Write "Website A is the best option because...", not "Website A is the better overall pick".
167	- **Straight apostrophes and quotes only** (`'` `"`). Never curly ones (`’` `“`). This was flagged on 3987088, 3979081, 3988061 and 3991159.
168	- **One paragraph per reason**, with no line breaks (3979081).
169	- **Third person only.** No "I", "me", "my" or "we".
170	- **No stiff connecting words** like "therefore", "thus", "hence", "moreover", "furthermore" or "additionally". Use "so", "but" and "and", or start a new sentence.
171	- No em dashes, and no filler like "seamless", "elevate" or "robust".
172	- **Never write "neither has a weak spot"**, "neither has a flaw" or "nothing is broken" (3979081).
173	- **No contradictions.** Don't call a site complete or equal while listing things it lacks (3991159).
174	- Only facts confirmed on screen (see 3.4). Don't mention how the sites were checked.
175	
176	### 4.2 Allowed openings
177	The verdict comes first, with no category words:
178	- Website A is better because...
179	- Website A is the best option because...
180	- Website A is preferred because...
181	- Website A is stronger because...
182	- Ties: **Both Website A and Website B are good because...** or **Both Website A and Website B are bad because...**
183	
184	Rotate the openings from task to task. The rest of each sentence should also vary in rhythm.
185	
186	### 4.3 Templates
187	Each reason is one paragraph of 4–6 sentences and **80–110 words**. Use concrete on-screen words: colors, shapes, section names, button labels, exact messages.
188	
189	**Aesthetics: Website X**
190	1. **Verdict and the main reason:** "Website X is better because its [main visual] [does what]."
191	2. **The winner's look, with three or more concrete details:** the main visual and how it's drawn, colors, layout or frame, title treatment.

# UI Berry: Website Preference Tasks

## 1. What I Provide
- A **Task ID**. The folder with that name holds the task HTML (instructions and the User request) and the saved files for Website A and Website B. Sometimes they come zipped.
- Screenshots of both websites (optional, and often cut off).
- Reviewer feedback from earlier tasks in `Prompt/Feedback.md`. Read it before every task.

When a new Task ID comes in, work only from that folder. Never reuse content from a previous task.

**Per-task workflow:**
1. Evaluate (section 3).
2. Write the three reasons with the templates (section 4).
3. Run the final checklist (section 6).
4. Give the answer in one code block, and append it to the end of `Feedback.md` with an empty `## Feedback:` slot.
5. When feedback arrives, add a row to section 7 and update the rules.

---

## 2. Task Types

### Type 1: Aesthetics / Functionality / Overall
Three independent picks. Each one is **A is better / B is better / Both are good / Both are bad**.
- **Aesthetics:** visual quality only: layout, composition, typography, color, polish, spacing and visual defects. Ignore whether controls work.
- **Functionality:** behavior and prompt-following only. Does the requested content render, and do the links, buttons, controls, navigation and interactions work? Ignore polish unless broken rendering blocks the check.
- **Overall:** the complete experience, weighing looks and behavior together. It doesn't have to match the other two picks.

### Type 2: Editing A/B Preference (Before / After)
Two independent picks: **Satisfaction** and **Overall**.
- Each tab (Website A, Website B) shows a split screen with **Before Edit** on the left and **After Edit** on the right. Judge the **After Edit** side. The Before page is usually the same for both.
- **Satisfaction:** does the After site do what the edit request asked? Are the requested parts there, and do they work? Ignore polish unless it blocks use.
- **Overall:** the **whole After website**, not just the new feature. That covers the hero section, images, navigation bar, every section, all buttons and the requested feature, and how they look and work together.

### Which file is which
In the task HTML, the first iframe sits in the "Website A" tab and the second in the "Website B" tab. Usually Website A is `saved_resource.html` and Website B is `saved_resource(1).html`. For editing tasks, open each wrapper file to find its Before and After files.

A site that fails to load, freezes or can't be inspected counts as a **functionality failure**.

---

## 3. How to Evaluate

### 3.1 Start with the request
Turn the User request into a checklist of every concrete requirement:
- elements and content
- colors and style
- modes
- behaviors
- limits, for example "just one page"

Check every item on both websites.

### 3.2 Test the way the reviewer does
Reviewers use each site inside the task page: a frame about **1000px wide and 800px tall**. Editing panes are only about **480–680px wide**. Test there, with real mouse clicks, hovers, drags and key presses.
- Click **every** button, tab, filter, toggle, card, tile and menu item, and note what each one does. Note the ones that do nothing. Footer and legal links only need one quick pass (see 3.6).
- **Check that each control changes the thing it claims to change, not just a label.** Compare the affected element before and after:
  - A chart's range buttons must redraw the line and the value axis, not only swap the date labels (3991159: Website B's period buttons only changed the dates).
  - A filter must change the list.
  - A Pause button must stop the updates and change every status label.
- Make sure menu items and buttons can be clicked across their whole area.
- Hover **every** tooltip, bubble and hotspot.
- Open **every** gallery or collection item and look at each card up close for overlaps, cut-off text and broken labels.
- On forms, try blank input and bad input. Note any warning text shown inside the form; that counts as an explanation (3979206).
- On games and tools, run the core loop once in **each requested mode**.
- Take one full-size look for the overall visual impression.

### 3.3 Build a control inventory (mandatory)
Before deciding anything, write a side-by-side list of **every control and feature on each site**, and mark each one:
- **Shared**: both have it and it works on both.
- **Only on Website A** or **only on Website B**: name it exactly, for example "an All resources filter on the schedule".
- **Broken or half-working**: say exactly what fails, for example "the period buttons only change the dates".

The inventory decides Functionality and keeps Overall honest. One extra working control can be the whole reason one site wins:
- 3979206: Website A's extra "All resources" filter decided Functionality.
- 3991159: Overall was marked down for saying Website A covered everything while naming features only Website B had.

### 3.4 What counts as evidence
- **Only what a reviewer sees on screen in normal use**, within a minute or two of clicking or playing. Describe longer flows through what's visible: scoreboards, buttons, rules text, targets.
- **Never use as evidence:**
  - Whether a file download works. Downloads are blocked in the review frame. A menu item that can't be clicked is still a valid point.
  - Phone or mobile layout.
  - Timing or speed numbers.
  - Console messages.
  - Flaws that only show at one window size.
  - **Anything learned from the code or network traffic**, such as endpoints called, FormData, or how a game is programmed (1210318).
  - **Anything that depends on saved browser storage**, such as a best score or draft kept after a reload (3978133).
- **Broken or missing images:**
  - If a picture the page loads right away is missing, the reviewer sees it broken too. This means a broken-image icon, alt text, or an empty box where a photo should be.
  - That counts as a Functionality failure, and as an Aesthetics flaw when it leaves a visible hole (3988061).
  - Images marked `loading="lazy"` that are missing on **both** sites are a saving gap, not a site flaw. Judge the layout around them and leave them out of the reasons.
- **Normal production patterns are not flaws.** Text clipped inside a short timeline bar, ellipses in tight table cells and similar compact UI are normal (3979206: cut-off names in one-hour bars weren't accepted as a flaw).
- **Measure before comparing sizes.** Never call an element "tiny" or "bigger" from a scaled-down screenshot (3978133).
- **A feature both sites have is never a difference.** Before crediting one site, confirm the other doesn't have it too.
- **Look again before calling something an advantage.** If it could be read as a flaw, leave it out.
- **Look again before calling something a failure.** If the site showed a warning or reason anywhere on screen, it explained itself (3979206).
- **Only quote text that is visibly on screen.** Screen-reader-only text (hidden live regions, `sr-only` labels, `aria-label`s) doesn't count. Before quoting a message, confirm it appears in a screenshot (3992127: "Hint names the exact row and column" came from hidden text; on screen the hint only highlights the piece and its space).
- **Describe visuals exactly as a screenshot shows them.** Check colors, positions and which element moves before writing about them. Never infer relationships, such as "a plate inside a turning ring", when the badge actually sits at the plate's corner (3987199). Never call a white header with a green button a "bold green header" (3992127).
- **Zoom into every photo and illustration at full size** to look for artifacts: rainbow or color-banding patches, smeared AI details, distorted text, stretched images. These are the clearest visual flaws (3987199: rainbow patches in Website B's photos were missed).
- **Don't over-claim.** Describe only what was actually shown.

### 3.5 What to check under each lens

**Aesthetics**
- Match to the requested look: colors, style and shape.
- The main visual (hero, logo, model, chart, character), with a specific detail of how it's drawn. For example: "a crate drawn as a flat dark green silhouette with only the carrot in color".
- The frame and page style: a dark cabinet or frame, the title treatment, the page background color (3978133).
- Layout and spacing: crowded areas, alignment, balance. Look for **uneven columns and empty gaps**, like a card that ends early and leaves a blank area while the next column keeps going (1210318).
- Typography and readability: text over photos, pale labels fading out, contrast.
- Visible defects: overlaps, cut-off text, wrong labels, elements covering content, broken images.
- Consistency and polish across sections, cards and icons.

**Functionality**
- Each item on the request checklist: is it present, and does it work?
- Each control named with its real result, checked as in 3.2.
- Dead or half-working controls named exactly: "code tiles do nothing on click", "the period buttons only change the dates".
- Options counted: "three backgrounds and an SVG-only download".
- Working features only one site has, taken from the inventory in 3.3.
- Navigation: menu links, tabs and pages actually open.
- Forms: blank and invalid input are rejected or explained.
- **Status labels that don't match the real state** are bugs, for example a "Live" or "Running" label shown while paused (1210318).
- Content that should show but doesn't: broken images, empty panels.
- **Visual details never go in Functionality.**

**Satisfaction (editing tasks)**
- Each requested change is in the After site, works with a real click and does the whole job.
- Ignore polish unless it blocks use.

**Overall**
- Cover the whole site: hero, images, navigation bar, sections, all buttons and the requested features.
- Weigh at least one visual point against at least one behavior point.
- Credit the other site's unique strengths **as unique**. Never write "matches it feature for feature", "covers everything the other has" or "does everything Website B does" unless the inventory shows that's literally true (3991159).

### 3.6 Decision rules
- Each question is judged on its own. Overall can differ from the others.
- Decide by the **biggest real difference in that lens**, not by counting nitpicks.
- **Functionality:** a working extra control on one site, or a broken or half-working control on the other, decides it (3979206, 3991159, 1210318).
- **Aesthetics:** a real visible defect decides it: a broken image, an empty gap, an overlap or unreadable text. Different styles, or normal production compactness, are a tie: **Both are good** (3979206).
- **Ties** only when the inventory shows no real difference and neither site has a real visible defect. Ties held on 3987088, 3979081 and 3979206 (Aesthetics). They were overturned on 1210318, where a real defect existed.
- **Every site has a weak spot.** Write one down for each site before deciding.
- When Aesthetics and Functionality both go to the same site, Overall usually goes there too.
- The option picked in the form must match the reason.

### 3.7 Steps to skip or keep short
**Skip:**
- Testing file downloads. Only check that the button or menu item can be clicked.
- Phone or mobile screenshots.
- Measuring timing or speed.
- Reading console warnings.
- Automatic overlap scanners. Look at close-up screenshots instead.
- Hunting for flaws at many window sizes.

**Keep short:**
- One full-size look for the overall impression. The review-frame check is the one that counts.
- One quick pass over footer, legal and "About" links.
- Read the site's code only when it saves time. For example, compare Before/After source on editing tasks, or check `loading="lazy"` on missing images.
- Play each game mode's core loop once. No need to play to the end.

---

## 4. How to Write the Three Reasons

### 4.1 Hard rules (each one has cost points)
- **Name the sites exactly "Website A" and "Website B"** every time. Never "Web Site A", "website a", "A", "B", "A's", "Site A", "Candidate 1" or "Website 1" (3991159, 3987088).
- **Name both sites in every reason.**
- **The first sentence is the verdict.**
- **Never address or name the reader.** No "you", "your", "users", "user", "visitors" or "people". Describe what the site does instead. Write "the leaderboard keeps every row tagged Running", not "it tells users every strategy is running" (3991159).
- **No category names inside a reason.** Don't write "aesthetics", "aesthetic", "functionality", "functional", "function", "overall" or "satisfaction" in the text. The field label already says it (3991159). Write "Website A is the best option because...", not "Website A is the better overall pick".
- **Straight apostrophes and quotes only** (`'` `"`). Never curly ones (`’` `“`). This was flagged on 3987088, 3979081, 3988061 and 3991159.
- **One paragraph per reason**, with no line breaks (3979081).
- **Third person only.** No "I", "me", "my" or "we".
- **No stiff connecting words** like "therefore", "thus", "hence", "moreover", "furthermore" or "additionally". Use "so", "but" and "and", or start a new sentence.
- No em dashes, and no filler like "seamless", "elevate" or "robust".
- **Never write "neither has a weak spot"**, "neither has a flaw" or "nothing is broken" (3979081).
- **No contradictions.** Don't call a site complete or equal while listing things it lacks (3991159).
- Only facts confirmed on screen (see 3.4). Don't mention how the sites were checked.

### 4.2 Allowed openings
The verdict comes first, with no category words:
- Website A is better because...
- Website A is the best option because...
- Website A is preferred because...
- Website A is stronger because...
- Ties: **Both Website A and Website B are good because...** or **Both Website A and Website B are bad because...**

Rotate the openings from task to task. The rest of each sentence should also vary in rhythm.

### 4.3 Templates
Each reason is one paragraph of 4–6 sentences and **80–110 words**. Use concrete on-screen words: colors, shapes, section names, button labels, exact messages.

**Aesthetics: Website X**
1. **Verdict and the main reason:** "Website X is better because its [main visual] [does what]."
2. **The winner's look, with three or more concrete details:** the main visual and how it's drawn, colors, layout or frame, title treatment.
3. **Another strength of the winner,** for example a section style, card design or readability.
4. **The other site's specific visible problem:** a broken image, empty gap, overlap, unreadable text, or a clear mismatch with the requested style. Name where it is.
5. **One honest weak spot of the winner,** kept small.

*Tie version:* "Both Website A and Website B are good because..."
- Describe each site's style with two or three concrete details.
- Name one specific weak spot for each site.
- End with why those don't change the call.

**Functionality: Website X**
1. **Verdict and the deciding behavior:** "Website X is stronger because [the control or behavior that decides it]."
2. **The winner's controls and their results:** three to five, each named with what it does.
3. **Shared features stated as shared:** "Both sort the leaderboard, filter by..., and...".
4. **The other site's exact gap:** a missing control named exactly, or a broken one with what happens. For example: "Website B's period buttons only change the dates on the chart."
5. **One honest weak spot of the winner,** if there is one.

*Tie version:*
- List the shared working features.
- Give each site's extra and one weak spot for each.
- Never include visual words.

**Overall: Website X** (write it last)
1. **Verdict:** "Website X is the best option because [deciding factor]."
2. **Fair credit to the other site,** with its real strengths named. Call its unique features unique.
3. **The winner's visual point:** one concrete detail.
4. **The winner's behavior point:** one control and its result.
5. **Why the deciding factor outweighs the other site's strengths,** with the winner's own small weak spot kept in proportion.

Overall must not repeat the Functionality sentences or say "matches everything".

### 4.4 Example (3991159, rewritten to the rules)
Functionality: Website A

The period buttons redraw the equity line and its value axis for each range, Pause scanner switches the trade feed badge to Paused, and the filter panel can also narrow strategies by type. Both sites sort the leaderboard, filter by market, timeframe, win rate, drawdown and trade count, compare two strategies side by side and run backtests. Website B's period buttons only change the dates under its chart, and every strategy row keeps a green Running tag after scanning is paused.

---

## 5. Answer Format
Write the whole result in **one code block**.

Aesthetics / Functionality / Overall tasks:
```
Aesthetics: Website B
Reason paragraph

Functionality: Website A
Reason paragraph

Overall: Website A
Reason paragraph
```

Editing tasks:
```
Satisfaction: Both are good
Reason paragraph

Overall: Website B
Reason paragraph
```

All of these have cost points. If the text gets edited, re-run the checklist below.

- [ ] A control inventory was made (3.3), and each control's real effect was checked, not just its label (3.2).
- [ ] Each reason opens with the verdict, using an allowed opening (4.2).

- [ ] Every failure claim was double-checked for an on-screen warning or explanation.

- [ ] No claims from code, network, storage, downloads, phone layouts or timing. Lazy-loading gaps shared by both sites are left out.
- [ ] Each page was checked for broken images, empty gaps, uneven columns and status labels that don't match the state.
- [ ] Ties are used only when nothing real separates the sites, and each tie names one weak spot per site.
- [ ] Each reason is 80–110 words (never under 40), counted.
- [ ] The opening style differs from the previous task.
- [ ] The pick in the form matches the reason.

  - Matches: a long white and light grey printer body, the print-head carriage on its rail, and a side panel whose small screen reads "READY TO PRINT" with buttons. It also has an angled stand on locking casters and a bottom roller with orange end caps.

content.text:
The decision is clear, with one correction to my earlier notes. Website A's accent is #ee613b and Website B's coral is #e95743, which are nearly the same red-orange. So I won't count the accent color against Website A. The difference is that Website B also offers a cobalt blue option.

Website B wins all three for 6241898. Website A is "Forma 1600" (saved_resource.html) and Website B is "Forma X1" (saved_resource(1).html). Both sites were tested in the 800px review frame with real clicks.

**Website A**
- Its large, detailed printer has a curved banner that hangs naturally.
- The print is so washed out that the pink, yellow and cyan barely show.
- Every control works: drag, the ± and scroll zoom, auto-rotate, Studio and Wireframe, the Isometric, Front and Side cameras, Reset, Expand and the print-head hotspot. The spec tabs, application dialogs and contact form work too.
- Its spec tab lists 13.6k triangles.

**Website B**
- Its isometric printer sits centered in a card, with a vivid cyan, yellow and pink banner and a coral stripe.
- Every control works: three accents (Coral, Cobalt, Graphite), three banner designs (Spectrum, Ocean, Monochrome), wireframe, grid, the camera menu, auto-rotate, Reset, Expand, Save to My collection, and the license, about and quick-start dialogs.
- Its specs list 5,282 triangles.
- Weak point: the Side view shows the banner is a flat sheet, not curved.

**Tie, so left out of the reasons:** both download buttons are blocked in the review frame, and both still show a false "downloaded" or "ready" message.

Written for: the task reviewers. Each reason is 60 words, in third person, with a different opening from the last task.

Aesthetics: Website B
```
Website B is better because its isometric printer sits centered in a soft grey card, and the banner carries a vivid cyan, yellow and pink gradient under white MAKE IT BIG lettering, with a coral stripe running along the body. Website A's printer is larger and its banner curves nicely, but the print is so pale it reads almost white.
```

Functionality: Website B
```
Website B is stronger because its controls change the model: Coral, Cobalt and Graphite recolor the accent stripe, Spectrum, Ocean and Monochrome swap banner prints, and the camera menu snaps to Isometric, Front or Side. Saving adds it to My collection. Website A's views, zoom and hotspot work, but its banner gradient barely shows the requested pink, yellow and cyan.
```

Overall: Website B
```
Website B is the better overall choice. Website A's curved banner hangs more naturally, and Website B's banner shows as a flat sheet in Side view. Still, Website B's vivid pink, yellow and cyan print, centered isometric framing, lighter 5,282-triangle model against Website A's 13.6k, and working accent and banner options clearly outweigh that one advantage for a hero section.
```

For task 3983197 (PNW Anime Wraps shop), Aesthetics is a tie and Website B wins Functionality and Overall. It was a close call, so the two calls I'd most want to know the reviewer's view on are below.

Website A is saved_resource.html and Website B is saved_resource(1).html. Both sites' main hero photo is missing from the saved files, so that gap is even and I left it out of the reasons. Every control below was tested with real clicks in the review frame, checking what it actually changed.

| | Website A | Website B |
|---|---|---|
| Shared | Hero with Shop Automotive / Shop Apparel buttons; category cards that filter the products; sort; quick view; Add to Cart with a cart drawer and quantity buttons; load more; demo checkout; search; newsletter that rejects a blank email; product hover with lift, red glow and image zoom; footer info windows | Same |
| Only here | Filter bar pinned the whole way down the page; subcategory links (Hoodies … Bonnies, Keychains … Mugs) under each category card; size guide and vinyl installation windows; Name A–Z sort | Three-slide hero carousel with a new headline per slide; heart button that saves to a Saved tab ("2 products"); account panel; crew code field; subcategories in the header hover menus |
| Broken | None found | None found |
| Weak spot | Character art mostly gray and white; no wishlist or account | Automotive tile only as tall as the Decals tile, while the brief says it must dominate; subcategories only in the header menus |

**Two judgment calls to flag:**
- **Aesthetics tie:** Website A follows the "Automotive must be the largest card" rule more clearly, and Website B has the brighter anime look. If you think the brief's "MUST" outweighs style, Aesthetics could go to Website A instead.
- **Functionality to Website B:** Website A also has unique pieces, mainly the guide windows and the filter bar that stays pinned for the whole page. I gave it to Website B because its wishlist, account panel and carousel are shopping features a reviewer will notice right away.

All three reasons pass the checks: one paragraph each, straight quotes, 112–114 words, "Website A/B" spelled exactly, and no reader or category words.

```
Aesthetics: Both are good
Both Website A and Website B are good because each one looks like a dark, aggressive car-culture shop built on black panels and bold red accents. Website A opens with a big white PNW logo block, and its huge Automotive tile towers over the smaller Decals and Windshield Banners tiles, just as the brief asks. Website B brings brighter anime energy, with glowing red Akuma eyes, a pink-haired anime sticker, large Japanese kanji behind the hero text and a row of trust icons under it. Website A's character art is mostly gray and white, and Website B's Automotive tile is no taller than the Decals tile, but neither issue changes the call.

Functionality: Website B
Website B is stronger because it adds more working shopping tools on top of the same core store. Its hero arrows step through three featured collections, the heart on each product saves it to a Saved tab that lists the saved items, and the account icon opens a profile panel. Both sites filter products from the category cards, sort by price, open a quick view, add items to a cart drawer with quantity buttons, load more products and open a demo checkout. Website A adds size guide and vinyl installation windows and subcategory links under each card, but it has no wishlist or account. Website B's subcategories only show up in the header menus.

Overall: Website B
Website B is the best option because it pairs a louder anime look with the deeper set of working shop tools. Website A has real strengths of its own, like an Automotive tile that clearly dominates the category section, a filter bar that stays pinned the whole way down the page, and size and vinyl installation guides. Website B answers with bright red and pink anime artwork, kanji accents and a trust strip under the hero, plus a three-slide hero, a wishlist with its own Saved tab and an account panel. Its Automotive tile is no taller than its neighbors, but the extra tools and stronger anime energy give Website B the edge.
```
